#9704. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9703. The AI Delegation Ladder: How Software Development Roles Are Evolving

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

You’re learning to build software faster with AI. What happens to your role when you can delegate an entire application, or fulfill the user’s request without building one?

Consider a sales manager who needs a customer retention report. First, you build the reporting app with AI assistance. Next, you specify its behavior, and AI generates it. Further ahead, AI could assemble the report directly through the company’s existing tools.

The AI Delegation Ladder for Software Development describes this possible evolution. Each step expands what we delegate and shifts the skills developers need.

The shift in skills: designing systems → specifying behavior → designing experiences and integrations.

The roles below describe how existing engineering responsibilities could evolve with that shift.

You direct implementation and review the changes. AI handles coding tasks.

You choose the database, design the architecture, and define how the reporting app fits the company’s systems. AI helps implement queries, interfaces, tests, and deployment scripts. You review the changes and remain responsible for the result.

The reporting dashboard may look finished while counting revenue twice or exposing customer data. Generating code quickly makes the judgment needed to evaluate it more valuable.

Roles that evolve: The Full-System Architect owns design decisions across the stack; the AI DevOps Engineer builds and operates the coding agents, evaluation pipelines, deployment, and monitoring that support delivery.

Design and architecture: Reason across the full system. Understand how interfaces, services, data, security, and operations affect one another.

Technical breadth and quick learning: Compare tools and frameworks, fill knowledge gaps through documentation and prototypes, and make informed decisions. Give coding agents clear tasks and validate the results.

The next step is to delegate the entire application.

You define requirements and verify behavior. AI generates the application.

For the same reporting app, you specify business rules, data definitions, access policies, and acceptance criteria. AI makes implementation choices within those constraints. Your work focuses on ensuring the system meets its requirements.

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

What counts as a declining account? Do refunds reduce revenue? Can a regional manager see customers from another region? Each unanswered question leaves AI to choose an interpretation.

“Requirements compiler” is a metaphor: business requests lack the precision of a compiler’s input. Tests can also miss a mistaken interpretation. Delegating implementation requires stronger specifications and assurance.

Roles that evolve: The Product Engineer translates business intent into testable requirements; the Software Assurance Engineer establishes confidence in the generated system through verification, security checks, and runtime monitoring.

Requirements and domain modeling: Turn business intent into explicit rules, resolve ambiguity, and define acceptable behavior.

Verification: Design meaningful acceptance tests, challenge edge cases, and decide what evidence is sufficient for the risk involved. Detailed code review may still be necessary for critical components.

The next step questions whether the report needs a dedicated app at all.

You design the experience and integrations. AI assembles and executes the workflow.

“Analyze customer purchases over the last six months, identify declining accounts, and prepare a retention report.”

AI retrieves authorized data, invokes analytical tools, and returns the report. The task runs through existing services, without building a dedicated reporting application.

AI becomes a shared backend for different user experiences, translating requests into tool and service calls. Databases, calculation engines, and access controls still do the underlying work. Developers provide reliable integrations and interfaces that let users guide the process.

Roles that evolve: The AI Experience Engineer designs how people request, understand, and guide the work; the AI Integration Engineer connects the data, tools, and services that make it possible.

User experience: Help people express goals, inspect results, and guide the next step. Design interfaces that adapt to the task and keep users in control.

Integration: Connect AI to the right data, tools, and services. Make them work reliably together, with clear permissions and recovery when something fails.

This evolution can unfold at different speeds across projects. Recurring workflows may justify dedicated apps; critical systems may continue to require detailed code review. The skills accumulate: architecture and verification remain valuable as experience design and integration move to the foreground.

Every step up the delegation ladder changes what makes a developer valuable. Are your skills climbing with it?

HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. Key Features

Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. #9700. Java 方法的使用：定义、传参、重载与递归

方法就是把完成某个功能的代码放在一起，起一个名字，需要时通过这个名字调用。 同一段逻辑可以反复使用，也能把复杂任务拆成几个更容易理解的小任务。

理解一个方法，先看三件事：接收什么数据（参数）、完成什么操作（方法体）、交回什么结果（返回值）。 方法也可以没有参数，或者没有返回值。

定义方法不会自动执行方法体，调用才会执行；方法结束后，会回到调用处继续执行。 同一个方法可以被多次调用，每次使用这次传入的数据重新执行。

有返回值不代表一定要用变量接收，但不使用它，就得不到这次计算的后续用途。 是否输出，取决于有没有执行打印语句。

在 main 中调用 int result = getSum(10) * 2;，先得到 55，再计算出 110。

因此，“类型匹配”不等于必须逐字相同。反过来，不能把一个 double 返回值直接赋给 int 变量。

条件表达式本身就是 true 或 false，可以直接返回。调用 System.out.println(isLeapYear(2024)); 会输出 true。

执行到 return 就会结束本次方法调用，不会继续向后执行。 对本章这些有返回值的方法，要保证每条可能正常结束的分支都能返回结果，不能只在某个 if 分支中返回，其他情况却没有返回值。

void 不表示“返回 0”，而是不返回任何值。这种方法可以执行到末尾结束，也可以使用不带值的 return; 提前结束。

选择返回值时，问自己：调用者是否还要使用计算结果？需要就返回；如果任务只是打印内容，不需要交回结果，就可以用 void。

例如，只有 getSum(int n) 时，getSum(10) 合法，而 getSum(10.9) 会编译失败，因为 double 不能直接传给 int 形参。

形参不要求与调用处的变量同名。add(a, b) 中的 a、b 与方法里的 x、y 是不同变量。

Java 始终按值传递参数。 对这里的 int 来说，复制的是整数值，x、y 不是 a、b 的别名，所以交换的是副本。

五次调用依次返回 1、2、6、24、120，相加得到 153。每次进入 factorial，都会重新创建并初始化自己的 result，不会沿用上一次的值。

这样写是把内部循环封装进方法，使任务更清楚；并没有消除内部循环，也没有自动减少运算次数。

两个整数相加、两个小数相加、三个小数相加，做的都是“相加”，没必要分别起三个名字。可以使用同一个方法名，通过参数列表区分。

本章在同一个类中判断重载：方法名相同，参数列表不同。 编译器根据调用处的参数个数和类型等信息，确定调用哪个方法。

前三种差异满足一种即可，并不是要求同时满足。把两个 int 形参换个位置，类型序列仍是 (int, int)，也不能构成重载。

返回值类型不参与重载的区分。 例如 double result = add(1, 2);，在上例中调用的仍是 add(int, int)，然后把返回的 int 转换成 double，不会因为左边是 double 就选择小数版本。

对于本章的普通方法，方法签名可以理解为“方法名 + 参数类型列表”，不包括形参名字和返回值类型。例如 add(int, int) 与 add(double, double) 的签名不同，所以可以重载。参见 Java 语言规范：方法签名。

编译后，.class 字节码中还会使用方法描述符记录参数类型和返回值类型。它与源代码层面的方法签名不是同一概念，也不是把方法名改成一个长名字。

可使用 JDK 自带的 javap 查看。先编译，再进入 .class 所在目录执行：

数组可以先理解为存放一组同类型数据的结构；这里的类名使用 / 分隔包名，记住 String 对应的写法即可，具体用法后续学习。

描述符包含返回值类型，并不意味着 Java 源代码允许仅凭返回值类型重载。 这两层规则要分开理解。参见 Java 虚拟机规范：方法描述符。

一个方法在执行过程中调用自身，就是递归。 它适合把原问题转化成“规模更小、解法相同”的子问题。

调用 factor(5) 得到 120。这个版本的输入要求是 n >= 1，不能传入 0 或负数，否则 n - 1 会不断远离出口；示例还要求结果不超出 int 范围。

return n * factor(n - 1); 不是遇到 return 就立刻跳走，而是先算出它后面的表达式，再把结果返回。因此，必须等待 factor(n - 1) 完成，才能乘以本层的 n。

每一层调用都有自己的 n。进入 factor(3) 不会把上一层的 n = 4 改成 3。

每次方法调用都会建立一个栈帧，保存这次调用的参数、局部变量、执行位置等信息；这些尚未结束的调用组成调用栈。

可以把它想成一叠记录纸：调用新方法时放上一张，方法返回时取走最上面一张，继续处理下面那张。因而，最后进入的方法先返回。

在最深处，调用关系是 main → factor(4) → factor(3) → factor(2) → factor(1)。factor(1) 返回后，恢复的是 factor(2)，不会直接跳过中间几层回到 main。在 IDEA 调试时，可以通过调用栈查看这些层次。

以下方法都写在类中，在 main 中调用。示例使用非负整数或正整数，具体范围见各题；计算结果需在 int 能表示的范围内。

对 1234，num / 10 得到前面的 123，num % 10 得到最后一位 4。要从左到右打印，就先处理前面的部分，再打印当前最后一位。

返回时依次打印 2、3、4。递归调用之前的代码在向下调用时执行，之后的代码在返回后执行。 如果把打印放到递归调用前，就会先打印末位，顺序变为 4、3、2、1。

这里没有显式写 return 作为出口：当 num <= 9 时，跳过递归调用，打印后方法自然结束。输入 0 也会正确打印 0。

对 1729，把问题拆成“最后一位 9 + 前面 172 的各位数字之和”。剩下一位数时，直接返回这个数。

注意两类题的区别：求 1 到 n 的和，每次用 n - 1；处理一个整数的各位数字，每次用 num / 10 去掉最后一位。

本题从第 1 项开始计数：1，1，2，3，5，8，13，...。前两项为 1，从第三项起，每项等于前两项之和，输入要求 n >= 1。

输入越大，重复计算越严重。计算一次 fib(40) 会得到 102334155，其中 fib(3) 会被调用 39088169 次。

若要统计次数，可以在类中、方法外定义 public static int count = 0;，并在 fib 的出口判断之后、递归调用之前加入：

count 是静态成员变量，这里只需理解为各次调用共同使用的计数器；每次重新统计前将其设为 0，调用结束后打印它。不能在 fib 内定义一个普通局部变量 count = 0 代替，因为每层调用都会有自己独立的计数。

递归适合表达问题的拆分关系，但不代表一定更高效。判断时既要看能否到达出口，也要看是否反复计算相同的子问题。

#9699. How Fake Job Interviews Helped Hackers Pull Off a $6.3 Billion Crypto Heist

Software Engineer and tech storyteller. I believe the best technical writing skips the victory lap and focuses on the struggle.

Software Engineer and tech storyteller. I believe the best technical writing skips the victory lap and focuses on the struggle.

Software Engineer and tech storyteller. I believe the best technical writing skips the victory lap and focuses on the struggle.

The job interview was real. The interviewers were not.

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, says hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (about £4.7bn) got in partly through fake job interviews.

One of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job site. The 'company representatives' he met were fake. They even shared social media accounts with personal photos to build trust.

In the second interview, he was asked to download an 'assignment'. It was malware.

Binance says the attackers then used his computer and an internal AI tool to take over two other engineers' laptops.

This is not a story about one careless person. These were patient, convincing people.

The lesson applies to everyone, not just engineers: a genuine platform does not make a genuine person. A job site can show that an account exists. It cannot tell you who is behind it.

Never install software or run a 'test' file just because a recruiter asked.

If a coding task has to be run, use a separate device, never your work laptop.

Check the company through its own website and phone number, not the links they send.

A real employer will not mind you checking.

The same lesson applies from the other side of the table. If your process includes a take-home task, make it something candidates can do in a browser or an online sandbox, not a file they have to download and run. Say clearly in writing what you will and will not ask them to install. Give them a named contact they can verify through your company website. Good candidates are learning to be careful. A process that respects that will look more trustworthy, not less.

When you have interviewed engineers, have you set take-home tasks, and how did you make sure candidates never had to run untrusted code on their own machines?

Source: BBC News, 'Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack' (3 November 2026)

#9697. 07 Java 调试案例讲解

调试（Debugging）就是查找并改正程序错误的过程。 核心是观察程序的实际执行过程，逐步缩小问题范围，找到“从哪一步开始，实际结果与预期不一致”。

以下使用 IntelliJ IDEA，Java 环境沿用课件中的 JDK 17。快捷键按课件的 Windows 键位说明；若自行修改过键位，以按钮提示为准。

红点表示断点位置，执行高亮表示程序当前停留的位置。判断某个结果为什么还没出现，先检查产生结果的语句是否已经执行。

变量区显示当前选中方法中的变量及其值。例如，停在 main 中可以查看 a、b；进入 add 后，可以查看 x、y。

表示 main 调用了 add，当前正在执行 add，main 正在等待它返回。最上方通常是当前执行的方法，下面是调用它的方法。

点击不同的方法记录，可以查看该次调用对应的变量。后面的数字是代码行号，不是调用次数。

程序暂停时，在 Debugger 中的 Evaluate expression ... or add a watch 输入区域填写表达式，按回车可查看结果。

表达式中的变量必须在当前查看的位置可用。例如选中 add 时使用 x、y，选中 main 时使用 a、b。

只有输出语句执行之后，Console 才会出现对应内容。程序停在 System.out.println(ret); 这一行时，并不表示 30 已经打印。

停在断点 A 时按 F8，add(a, b) 会正常执行。到达下一行 System.out.println(ret); 时：

步过只是通常不进入方法内部逐步查看，方法本身仍然执行。 如果方法内部另有断点，也可能在内部停下来。

如果刚进入 add 就使用步出，剩余的打印和 return 仍会执行，然后回到 main 的调用位置。

步出不会取消这次调用，也不会丢掉剩余代码。 返回后界面可能仍高亮调用所在行，继续单步即可观察后续赋值和输出。

普通 F7 可能按调试器的过滤规则跳过某些 Java 类库方法，例如 System.out.println() 的内部实现。确实需要查看这些方法时，可以使用 Alt + Shift + F7。

“强制”是指绕过普通步入的过滤规则，并不意味着任何方法都一定有可供查看的源码。本章只需掌握它与普通步入的区别。

程序停在断点 A 时，按 F9（Resume Program），程序继续正常执行，命中断点 B 后暂停。此时 ret = 30，但 30 尚未打印。

例如停在断点 A 时，把光标放到 System.out.println(ret);，执行后会在这行暂停，便于查看 ret。

目标位置之前的代码仍会执行；如果途中先命中其他断点，会先在那个断点暂停。目标行也必须是本次执行能够到达的位置。

Ctrl + F2 是停止，不是可继续执行的暂停。 停止之后，要再次运行就需要重新启动。参见 IDEA 调试会话说明。

禁用适合暂时保留某个断点，删除适合不再需要的断点，屏蔽适合临时让程序不因这些断点而停下。

循环执行很多次时，普通断点会反复暂停。如果只想检查 i == 20 的情况，可以设置条件断点。

条件应是结果为 true 或 false 的表达式。这里写 i == 20，不是赋值表达式 i = 20，也不需要写 if 或分号。

调试时每一步都应带着一个检查目标：输入是否正确、哪一步计算有误、返回结果是否符合预期。 找到第一个出现偏差的位置，通常就能明显缩小错误范围。

#9696. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi/T)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​/T)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80:

C=3(0.99)−12=0.98 C=\frac{3(0.99)-1}{2}=0.98 C=23(0.99)−1​=0.98

Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

#9695. CMAK exposes Kafka cluster administration through a separate control plane

CMAK, formerly Kafka Manager, is a web application for managing Apache Kafka clusters. It stores cluster connection settings and presents topic, consumer group, partition, and broker operations through a browser. The application is not the Kafka broker, but it can hold credentials and issue administrative requests on the broker's behalf.

The CMAK configuration supports basic authentication and LDAP-backed authentication. These controls protect the CMAK application. They do not automatically map every CMAK user to a narrow Kafka ACL. The Kafka client configured inside CMAK may use a service credential, a SASL identity, or a TLS certificate that is shared by everyone who reaches the UI.

That distinction is the main review point. A user who cannot connect to Kafka directly may still be able to perform an operation through CMAK if the application's broker credential is broad. The effective permission is the intersection of the CMAK authorization, the Kafka principal, and the operation the UI exposes. If CMAK has one administrator identity for all users, the Kafka ACL cannot distinguish them.

Inventory every configured cluster and the principal used for each connection. Record whether the connection is read-only, whether it can alter topics or consumer groups, and which Kafka ACLs apply. Separate production and non-production clusters. Test a view-only CMAK user against a topic creation or partition change path, including a direct HTTP request rather than only the visible button.

Protect the configuration and secret files. CMAK can store broker credentials in its configuration. A file that is readable by the application process should not be readable by every local user. Rotate the Kafka credential when an administrator leaves or when the CMAK deployment is rebuilt. A backup that contains the connection secret should be protected like the live configuration.

The network position matters because CMAK is a control plane. Place it on a management network or behind an identity-aware proxy, bind it to the intended address, and restrict outbound access to the configured Kafka clusters. An open proxy path from CMAK to arbitrary hosts can turn a management UI into a useful foothold during an incident.

The evidence for this article is a count-only ZoomEye observation. The query was title="CMAK", with sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1, observed at 2026-11-10T22:43:49Z. It returned 1,508 matching records. The query found an exact-title footprint; it does not prove that each result is CMAK, that authentication is disabled, or that the Kafka principal is privileged.

CMAK's convenience comes from holding Kafka authority in one place. That is also its risk. Limit who can use the UI, make the Kafka principal match the intended role, protect the stored credentials, and verify that the broker ACLs still enforce the boundary when the UI is bypassed.

#9693. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9692. Why AI Is Making Everything Look and Sound the Same

AI CTO and systems builder. CTO of Archdesk; founder of Lextron.ai, Inclify and Rejsomat. I write on enterprise AI, agents and Joule Wars.

AI CTO and systems builder. CTO of Archdesk; founder of Lextron.ai, Inclify and Rejsomat. I write on enterprise AI, agents and Joule Wars.

AI CTO and systems builder. CTO of Archdesk; founder of Lextron.ai, Inclify and Rejsomat. I write on enterprise AI, agents and Joule Wars.

This autumn, one friend after another has shown me the apartment they're about to build. Different cities, different budgets, different lives. The same room. Pale oak slats on one wall. A boucle sofa the colour of oat milk. An arch where a door used to be, linen curtains, one olive tree in a pot, a pendant lamp like a paper moon. By the third render I stopped looking at the picture and asked to see the prompt. Each of them had asked ChatGPT to show them their future home. It showed all of them the same one.

None of them knew. How would they? Each had seen exactly one render, their own, and it looked like taste. I was the only person in the story who had seen the set.

I know how the complaint sounds. Every generation notices that the shops all sell the same thing and concludes that the young have no taste, and every generation is a little right and mostly just old. So I did what I do when a feeling won't leave: I went looking for measurements. I expected a few grumpy essays. I found a NeurIPS oral, a meta-analysis of 8,214 people, 22 million car sales and an experiment Spotify ran on its own users, and most of it points the same way. The sameness is real and you can count it, in interfaces, living rooms, playlists and scientific prose. Most of it is older than the machines. And the machines are speeding it up by a mechanism that nearly everyone gets wrong. I got it wrong myself until I read the papers.

In the first essay of this series I argued that technology never destroys value, it relocates scarcity: machines compress the middle of the capability distribution, and the returns run to the tails. I left out the strangest property of that compressed middle. It gets cheap, and then it gets identical.

I'm one of the people flooding the valley, again. I build with these systems every day and I'm not going to stop. So take what follows as a field report from inside the flood, with receipts, a table you can check row by row, and three bets I've put a number on.

Start with the machines on their own, before a human touches anything.

Ask a language model for a metaphor about time. Now ask it again, fifty times, with the randomness turned up. Then do the same with twenty-four other models, from other labs, trained on other data by people who compete with each other for a living. That's 1,250 attempts. A team ran exactly this for a paper called Artificial Hivemind, an oral at NeurIPS 2025, and what came back was two ideas. Time is a river. Time is a weaver. Two of the Qwen models produced the identical motto, word for word.

The full study threw 26,000 open-ended prompts at more than seventy models. A single model mostly repeated itself, and different models mostly repeated each other: cross-model similarity ran from 71 to 82 percent, and a typical cluster of fifty look-alike answers held the work of about eight different models. You can change your vendor. You'll get the same river.

None of this is new, only better measured. In January 2023 two researchers in Germany asked ChatGPT for a joke 1,008 times. More than 90 percent of what came back was the same 25 jokes, and one of them, about a scarecrow who won an award for being outstanding in his field, turned up 140 times. (Go and ask the chatbot in your other tab for a joke. I'll wait. If a scarecrow, a tomato or an atom is involved, you've just replicated a paper.)

The obvious reply is that people are no better. Ask a hundred humans about time and you'll hear about plenty of rivers. So a second team ran the comparison. Twenty-two models and 102 people took the same standard creativity tests. On the alternate-uses task, the one where you list things to do with an everyday object, the average distance between two humans' answers was 0.738. Between two models' answers it was 0.459. That gap is about two standard deviations, and a system prompt begging the models to "be very creative" closed less than half of it.

The detail I can't shake is that the models scored slightly higher than the people on individual originality. Any one answer was good, often better than yours or mine would have been. It was the set that was a monoculture.

You'd think there'd be a dial for this. Turn the temperature up, ask for something weird. But the Hivemind runs were already sampled hot. "Be very creative" bought back less than half the gap. A third team, comparing model-written book reviews with human ones, tried both tricks and barely moved their numbers. Temperature adds noise around the favourite answer. It doesn't change which answer is the favourite. To see why, you have to look at how these systems are finished, which is a different matter from how they're sampled.

The picture everyone reaches for, and the one I used myself, is the bell curve. The model learns the distribution of human work and hands you its middle. Everyone uses the same curve, so everyone gets the same middle. It's tidy, it's wrong, and the way it's wrong is the whole story.

Try it on my friends' living room. If you really averaged every living room on the internet you'd get a brown smear. The mean of a red sofa and a blue sofa is mud, and the mean of a thousand floor plans is fog. What ChatGPT drew was nothing like that. It was crisp and specific, a room you could order from a catalogue by Friday. An average is a blur of everything, and this was one particular thing. It wasn't averaged. It was picked.

The picking happens late. Pre-training teaches a model the whole messy distribution of what people have made, every cluster, with the empty space between them. Then comes post-training, the stage where people rate outputs and the model is tuned toward the ratings. That stage is an election, and it's held under a brutal rule. A 2025 paper from Meta's FAIR lab wrote the rule down: for the standard preference objective, putting all of the probability on the single highest-rated answer is an optimal solution. Winner takes all. And when two answers tie, moving everything onto one of them is still optimal, because the loss never looks at what was thrown away. (Real systems add a regularizer that stops the collapse from being total. It's a brake. The engine still pulls one way.)

So the oat-milk sofa is the candidate that won, under a system that gave the winner every seat. Averaging had nothing to do with it. The runner-up rooms, the ones with green velvet and terrible wallpaper, are probably still in the weights somewhere. They just never get called on.

The part that made me sit up was the fix. The same authors changed the objective to reward answers for being good and rare, and got about 75 percent more variety in stories and up to 46 percent more in invented personas, while winning head-to-head quality comparisons about as often as before. Which means the sameness is a default, the kind that stays put until somebody has a reason to change it.

Other groups have reached the same place from other directions. Take five models and compare each with its "aligned" chat version on a test of conceptual variety: alignment narrows every one of them, and none gets near the human baseline. Change nothing but the chat template, the role markers wrapped around your prompt, and variety drops anyway. And there's a finding that explains why switching vendors doesn't help, under the grand name of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (ICML 2024): as vision and language models get stronger, their internal representations converge on one another. Tolstoy would have recognised it. All strong models are alike; each weak model is weak in its own way.

So the honest version of my thesis is narrower than "AI averages culture," and I think worse: a handful of systems, finished by similar methods toward similar ratings, settle on the same winners, and then everybody draws their first draft from those winners. Tyler Cowen called his 2013 book Average Is Over. He was writing about the labour market. For the work itself I'd put it differently. The average isn't over. It's free, and nobody pays for what's free.

None of that would matter much if we treated a model as one voice in the room. The experiments say we don't.

The study that got to me came out of Wharton in 2025, in Nature Human Behaviour. Five experiments on brainstorming with ChatGPT. In one, people had to invent a toy using a brick and a fan. With the chatbot's help the individual ideas got better, as they nearly always do. But 94 percent of them overlapped with somebody else's, and nine participants, working independently, gave their toy the same name: "Build-a-Breeze Castle."

Think about those nine people for a second. Each of them, as far as they knew, had named a toy. Each had seen one answer. Only the researchers saw nine.

Across the five experiments, the pool of ideas was narrower with ChatGPT in 37 of 45 comparisons. The most varied ideas in the whole study came from people using nothing but their own heads and a web search.

One lab could be a fluke. The meta-analysis is harder to wave away: 28 studies, 8,214 participants. People working with generative AI do somewhat better work than people working alone (effect size +0.27). The variety of ideas across those same people falls off a cliff (effect size −0.86, and in social science you rarely see a number that size with a minus sign in front of it). If you keep one sentence from this essay, I'd like it to be the next one.

That is also why it's so hard to notice. Your own work really did improve, and you have the evidence in front of you. The cost turns up somewhere you can't see from your desk. It turns up in the set.

You can hear it happening to the language. A 2025 paper in Science Advances went through 15.1 million biomedical abstracts looking for words whose frequency suddenly broke from its own trend. At least 13.5 percent of the abstracts published in 2024 carried a language model's fingerprints, and in some sub-fields 40 percent. "Delves" appeared 28 times more often than its history predicted. The authors counted 454 such excess words in 2024, against 190 at the height of COVID. By that measure a chatbot bent scientific English about twice as hard as a pandemic did.

Then it got out of the text box. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute analysed 824,634 podcast episodes, the unscripted kind, and found the same vocabulary climbing in human speech. ChatGPT's favourite words were rising 25 to 50 percent a year, and "delve" beat a synthetic control at p = 0.01. Nobody pasted those sentences. People said them, with their own mouths, because a model had said them first. Listen for it in your next meeting.

The pull has a direction, too. In a controlled study of 118 writers in India and the United States, the same autocomplete suggestions nudged the Indian writers toward Western conventions, in what they said and in how they said it, and gave them smaller productivity gains for their trouble. Autocomplete has an accent, and it probably isn't yours.

Now count the people in the room. About forty percent of American adults had used generative AI by late 2024. OpenAI claimed 800 million weekly users in October 2025. Ahrefs found machine-written text in 74 percent of newly published English web pages, though only 2.5 percent were machine-written from top to bottom. Radio, television and the feed all distributed culture after someone had made it. This is the first medium that hands out the first draft, to most of the people making things, at the same moment, from a handful of sources that agree with one another.

The web is the easiest place to watch this, because the web can be crawled.

It was converging long before the models showed up. A CHI paper from 2021 measured how visually different website layouts were from one another and found the distance had fallen 43 percent between 2010 and 2019. Blame the frameworks. Bootstrap sits under three out of four sites whose CSS framework can be identified, and Tailwind is downloaded 176 million times a week. The interaction designer Boris Müller had the diagnosis in 2018, in one line: templates are content-agnostic, and that's the problem.

Then the generators arrived and the sameness grew a face. You know this page. Inter, or the system font. A hero section, centred, under a small pill-shaped badge that says something like "Now in beta." A gradient running from indigo to purple. Three feature cards in a row, icon on top. Rounded corners, a shadow at ten percent opacity, shadcn components straight out of the box. You may have shipped this page. I'm in no position to judge.

In August 2025 Adam Wathan, who created Tailwind, posted a half-serious apology. Five years earlier he had picked bg-indigo-500 as the default button colour in Tailwind UI. The default was copied into so many tutorials that the models learned it as what a button looks like, and now it's the complexion of the machine-made web: one person's offhand choice, laundered through a training set into the taste of a generation of startups. When a parody site of vibe-coded landing pages reached the Hacker News front page, the top comment was two words long. Mode collapse.

In April 2026 the joke became a measurement. A developer named Adrian Krebs pointed a headless browser at 1,590 recent Show HN launch pages and ran sixteen deterministic checks for exactly these tells. Twenty-two percent of the pages had four or more. Another 32 percent had two or three. (He puts his false-positive rate at five to ten percent.) So more than half of the startups launching on Hacker News that spring wore at least two fingerprints of machine-made design, and they wore them on the one page where a company tries hardest to look like nobody else.

The benchmark followed in October. Fifteen frontier models, eighty design briefs, 2,400 generated interfaces. Every model scored above 90 percent on appropriateness, so these are not bad pages. But on how distinct different models' answers to the same brief were, the models scored 0.59 where human designers scored 0.76. On creative range, meaning how differently one designer handles different briefs, the models managed 0.58 against the humans' 0.90. Fifteen different AIs, asked for fifteen different apps, produced work more alike than human designers given the same brief. I should say that the authors build UI-generation tooling, so hold the decimals loosely. The direction matches everything else here.

Each page is fine. That's the trouble. The set is one page.

Which brings me back to my friends, and to a prediction I keep hearing: soon every home will look the same inside. Most of the evidence here is older than AI, and I think that makes the case stronger. The machines found this already running and put their foot down.

Kyle Chayka gave the look a name in 2016: AirSpace, the chain of near-identical cafés, co-working lofts and Airbnbs, all subway tile and reclaimed wood and Edison bulbs, in cities that have nothing else in common. His evidence was anecdote. The market's isn't. In 2017 Zillow went through 32,000 listing photos and found that a "greige" exterior sold for about $1,500 more than expected. In 2023 it surveyed 4,700 buyers and found that a dark graphite kitchen added roughly $2,500 while a white one cost you $600. Six years apart the winning colour was grey both times, pale and then dark. People were being paid to converge.

Nobody chose greige. Greige is what's left when everyone stops choosing.

Scale handles the rest. IKEA has sold more than 140 million Billy bookcases, which is more bookcases than America has households. In American cities one paragraph of the 2000 International Building Code, section 510.2, allowed five storeys of timber frame on a concrete podium, and the "five-over-one" became the skyline of every boomtown: 450,000 apartments finished in 2023 alone, nearly all of them to rent. When computer-vision researchers built a system in 2012 to tell cities apart from single Street View frames, it learned Paris, London and Barcelona easily. It couldn't find anything distinctive to learn about American cities.

Cars are the cleanest record of taste we have, because every sale is logged and every colour is something a person paid for. In more than 22 million US vehicle sales, the four non-colours (white, black, grey, silver) went from 47 percent of model-year 1996 cars to 80 percent of model-year 2025 cars. In 1996 one new car in 28 was grey. Now it's one in four. Worldwide, the paint maker Axalta has had the same four at around 80 percent year after year, and its 2025 report puts them at 81. These are a supplier's figures, with the caveats that implies, but you can check them in any car park.

So this is what I think my friends were showing me. Take an image model trained on the photographs the market was already paying a premium for. Finish it with a process that crowns whichever answer the most raters like. Have three different people ask it for a warm, modern living room. Of course it drew one room. It drew the Zillow premium. Zillow itself now ships AI staging inside its listings, with a menu of approved looks for every empty room, and Pinterest likes to point out that 80 percent of its annual trend predictions come true, which is what tends to happen when you predict a trend and then show it to half a billion people until it does.

The render is a picture of what the raters agreed on, and the raters were us. Nobody in particular chose that home.

Each room is lovely. I mean that. The set is one room.

Music is where the gap between the desk and the set was first measured properly, by the company with the most to lose from the answer.

A randomized experiment on podcasts the same year caught the mechanism in the act. Personalized recommendations raised streams by 29 percent. They cut the variety of what each individual listened to by 11.5 percent. And they slightly raised variety across the user base as a whole. That's the dashboard problem in a single result. From headquarters everything looks more diverse than ever, while each person's world gets a little smaller.

Then the generators arrived on the supply side. When Deezer started detecting fully AI-generated tracks in January 2025, they were about 10 percent of what was delivered to the platform each day. By April 2026 they were 44 percent. In June 2026 they passed half, at around 90,000 tracks a day. Almost nobody listens to them (one to three percent of streams, and Deezer says up to 85 percent of those were fraudulent in 2025), but the catalogue's centre of gravity has moved. And a 2026 study that compared 20,000 Suno tracks with 20,000 human ones found the generator leaning even harder than pop does on the I–V–vi–IV progression, in a narrower harmonic space than the music it was trained on. It learned pop's one trick and plays it more often than pop.

The whole case fits in one table, so you can check it without rereading me, and so you can tell me which row is wrong. The sources are listed at the bottom of the page.

A fair objection by now: hasn't it always been like this? Mostly, yes. I went looking for the history and found plenty.

Print fixed spelling where manuscripts had let it wander. In 1926 the BBC convened a committee to settle how its announcers should pronounce things, while insisting it had no wish to standardize the nation's speech. Local American newspapers ran identical wire stories by the million. Between 1961 and 2009 the food supplies of 152 countries each got more varied at home and 36 percent more similar to one another, which is the whole pattern in miniature: more choice for everyone, less difference between anyone. And a 1994 art project that polled people in eleven countries about their ideal painting got back, again and again, the same blue landscape.

Each of those was a different machine: a shared press, a small centre setting a norm, a shared source, a shared supply chain. Culture has always had centres of gravity. So what's actually new?

Two things, I think. The first is that it's one machine now. Spelling had the printing press, pop had radio, kitchens had IKEA, and those were separate systems run by separate people with separate blind spots. A language model sits upstream of your cover letter, your landing page, your living room and your chorus all at once, and its rivals agree with it.

The second is where it sits. Radio shaped what you heard after it was made. A template shaped how you built something after you'd decided what to build. The model arrives before any of that, at the moment of the first idea, and the first idea is the one that sticks. Psychologists have a thirty-year-old experiment on this. Ask people to invent a creature from another planet, but first show them a few examples, all with four legs, antennae and a tail. Their creatures come back with four legs, antennae and a tail. Tell them explicitly to make theirs as different as possible and it doesn't help. We have now shown a few hundred million people the same example, at the same time, for everything.

An argument that can't say what would refute it is just a mood, so here is the best case against mine. It's better than I expected.

Fashion is the one domain someone has measured across more than 150 years of images, and it shows variety rising since the 1980s, with a crowd of niche looks replacing the single dominant one. Names went the same way: in 1955 American parents gave nearly a third of their sons a top-ten name, and by 2007 it was fewer than one in ten. National music charts on Spotify and iTunes drifted apart after 2017 when you'd have bet on them merging. People who take up streaming end up listening more widely than before. The genre map built from Spotify's own data counts more than 6,000 genres.

It gets closer to home. The collapse in human-AI work turns out to depend on the interface. When the model writes for you, variety falls. When it asks questions or offers options and the human stays in charge, quality goes up and variety holds; that's from a CHI 2026 study of more than a thousand people. Pay people for originality and the variety comes back, in two preregistered trials. The training collapse has a known fix. And the oldest result in this whole field, the MusicLab experiment of 2006, found that when its 14,341 participants could see each other's choices, hits became more unequal and less predictable. People herd, but where the herd ends up is close to a coin toss.

I accept all of it, and it narrows what I'm claiming. The free tier of everything becomes the same. The free tier is most of the volume. And the price of being visibly, legibly different from it goes up. Read that way, the counterexamples stop being exceptions. The niche label, the unusual name, the playlist somebody actually made: that's what the premium looks like when people pay it.

Back to the ladder. The Tail Premium says that when a technology compresses the middle of a distribution, the returns run to the ends. Everything above describes the compression, with one detail the first essay didn't have: the middle is crowded and it is also correlated. A million variations on one winner are one variation. So competence is no longer the scarce input, and "creativity" isn't quite it either, since the models do fine on individual originality. What's scarce is independence of source: an idea that didn't come from the same place as everyone else's.

The market already prices this, and the price has a shape. A 2025 paper in the Journal of Consumer Research scored 481,747 photos from New York Airbnb listings for visual uniqueness and matched them against occupancy. The curve was an inverted U. Listings that looked like every other listing were penalized. So were the truly strange ones. The best performers, by a margin worth thousands of dollars a year to a host, sat a measurable distance from the pack in a direction a guest could still read. That's the Tail Premium drawn as a curve: the rent goes to the room that is different on purpose and still makes sense, and the weirdest room does about as badly as the blandest. The grey car, seen this way, is a survey. It shows you where the margin went.

It also changes what a buyer can learn by looking. When artefacts converge, inspecting the artefact tells you less each year, and the question "who stands behind this, and what did they risk?" has to carry more of the weight. That's Human Signal. The number I expect to move is the Originality Premium, the price gap between work of verified origin and generated work in the same market, and it's the one I intend to measure.

What do you do about it on a Monday? I'm not going to tell you to stop using the tools. I won't, and you won't either. Using them costs you nothing. Accepting the first draft is the expensive part. So decide before you prompt: write down what you think, however badly, and only then ask. When you do ask for options, ask for twenty and bin the first five, because the first five are everybody's. And treat a model's defaults the way a decent cook treats a stock cube. Fine in an emergency. A confession on the menu.

The rule of this series is that an essay with nothing staked is an opinion in a nice jacket. So, three bets. They go on piszczek.pl/predictions with a commit hash before any of the windows open, each with a threshold, a deadline, a source that isn't me, and the outcome that proves me wrong. I've put a confidence on each, because I'd rather be calibrated than brave. If I say 80 percent and turn out right every time, I was sandbagging.

The third is the one I care about, so let me say it properly. Every era ends up named after whatever shaped its surfaces. We named most of a century after a queen and a decade after a school of design. We named a palette after a film stock and a face after an app. I think the 2020s get named after model families, because that's where most people making things drew their first draft. And I don't only mean pictures. A way of furnishing a room, a register of prose, a kind of chorus, a kind of face. People already say a poster looks "very Midjourney." The bet is that the habit leaves the trade and reaches things no model ever touched, until one day somebody describes a real kitchen, in a real house, with the name of a model, and everyone at the table knows exactly what they mean.

If these come in wrong, the essay was wrong, and I'll say so here in the same font size.

I don't know yet which of my friends will actually build the room in the render. Probably all of them, and I should be honest about why: it's a lovely room. That's how it won. It will photograph well, and nobody who visits will ever dislike it, which is a strange thing to be able to say about a place where a person lives.

So I'm not going to talk anyone out of the oak slats. If one of them asks, I'll say this, and I'll say it to you. Somewhere in the new place, keep one object that would lose every vote. Everybody owns one. The lamp from a grandmother's flat, in a colour that has no name. The chair that matches nothing. The painting a cousin made in a bad year. A model would never draw it, because no panel of raters would ever have agreed on it, and that's why it's worth more than the rest of the room put together. It's the only thing in there that couldn't have happened to anyone else.

Ask a machine what time is and you get a river. Ask it what home is and you get my friends' apartment. Tonight somebody, somewhere, is typing a warm, modern living room into a box, and the box is about to show it to them. They'll love it. They'll only ever see the one.

Scarcity never dies. It climbs. This time it climbed out of the product and into a smaller, odder question: whether the idea was yours before it was everyone's.

Lineage, because attribution is the point: Theodor Adorno on standardization in popular music (1941), Paul DiMaggio and Walter Powell on institutional isomorphism (1983), Matthew Salganik, Peter Dodds and Duncan Watts on social influence in cultural markets (2006), Jon Kleinberg and Manish Raghavan on algorithmic monoculture (2021), Kyle Chayka on AirSpace (2016) and Filterworld (2024), Alex Murrell on the age of average (2023), and Tyler Cowen on the end of average (2013). The sameness thesis is theirs. The measurements and the stakes are what I add.

Previous in this series: Scarcity Never Dies. It Climbs. Next: the price of checking, and the first measurement of the Originality Premium. The numbers land on this domain first.

How AI Is Making Creativity More Homogeneous

#9691. I built a desktop app where the AI agent can see your running app, not just your code

Piye is live on Mac and Linux. One project. Build it visually, or write the code.

After more than a year of building, Piye is live on Mac and Linux.

Piye is one desktop app where you build software visually or write the code, on the same project. This post is about the code side, because that's where most of the hard work went.

AI agents read your files, but they can't see what's actually happening: the error in the terminal, the breakpoint you hit, the crash on the phone simulator, the dev server that died. So they guess, explore the project again and again, and burn tokens doing it.

Piye Code is a full code editor, built from scratch rather than forked from another editor. Its own tools report to the agent:

Because the agent gets these reports directly, it spends less time searching and more time fixing the real problem. In one of our tests, it found the two causes of a performance bug in Piye's own code in 12 minutes, for about €2 of AI.

The agent never acts behind your back: commits, pushes and deploys each need your explicit approval.

On Piye's own credits, code work is charged at the AI's cost, so you're not paying a markup to write code.

A separate window for running many agents on many projects at once, showing which are running, done or waiting on you.

Founders can describe an app in Piye Visual and get a real website or a native iPhone, iPad and Android app, see it on real simulators, and publish to the web, the App Store and Google Play.

When they need a developer, Handoff creates a private GitHub repo and branch and writes a HANDOFF.md briefing: what's built, what's missing, which keys are needed. You open it in Piye, or in any editor you like. The project is a normal folder on your computer, with no lock-in.

Free on Mac and Linux, with 750 credits to start (no card): piye.dev

I'd really like honest feedback from developers: what's confusing, what breaks, what you'd need before using it every day.
