#9689. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#9688. 5 Small AI Projects That Actually Save You Time (and How to Build Each One)

Most AI demos show a model writing a poem or building a toy app in thirty seconds. Fun to watch, useless on Monday morning. The projects that actually pay off are smaller and more boring: they remove a repetitive task you already do every day, and they do it reliably enough that you stop thinking about it.

Here are five worth building. Each one takes an evening or a weekend, and each one comes with a concrete starting point — not a pitch, a plan.

What it does: Every morning at 8 a.m., you get one short digest: today's calendar, the three emails that actually need a reply, and the tasks you left unfinished yesterday.

Why it works: The value is not the summary. It is the triage. You stop opening five apps to figure out what today is.

How to build it: You don't need a framework. A small script that pulls your calendar events and unread emails, hands them to a language model with a strict instruction ("list only items that need a decision from me today, max 10 bullets"), and sends the result to yourself is enough. The key detail is the prompt: ask for decisions, not descriptions. A digest that says "you have 6 meetings" is noise. One that says "reply to Sara about the invoice before 11 a.m." is a brief.

Pitfall: Don't let it summarise everything. The moment the brief is longer than a phone screen, you stop reading it. Cap the output and let unimportant items drop silently.

What it does: You dump notes, links, meeting minutes and half-formed ideas into one folder. When you need something, you ask a question in plain language and get an answer with the source note attached.

Why it works: Search finds keywords. A second brain finds meaning — the note where you wrote "the client hates blue buttons" three months ago, even though you searched for "design feedback".

How to build it: Start embarrassingly simple. One folder of Markdown files, one script that embeds each file and stores the vectors, and a tiny query loop that retrieves the three most relevant notes and asks the model to answer using only those notes. Retrieval-augmented generation sounds fancy; in practice it is twenty lines of glue around an embedding API and a folder.

Pitfall: The system is only as good as the notes you actually write. If capturing a note takes more than ten seconds, you won't do it. Keep the capture step dumb — a single file you append to, no categories, no tags — and let search do the organising.

What it does: Incoming email gets classified — needs a reply, FYI, newsletter, noise — and for the ones that need a reply, a draft is written in your voice, waiting for your approval. Nothing is ever sent automatically.

Why it works: Writing the first draft is most of the work of replying. Approving or editing a draft takes a tenth of the time.

How to build it: Classification first, generation second. A simple rules pass (sender lists, subject keywords) handles the obvious 60%. The model handles the rest with a short prompt that includes two or three of your past replies as style examples. The non-negotiable rule: drafts sit in your drafts folder. The human sends.

Pitfall: Tone drift. If the model writes "Hope you're doing well!!" and you never would, the draft costs you more time than it saves. Feed it your real sent mail, and check the first twenty drafts before trusting the system.

What it does: Once a week it reads your analytics, your most-commented posts, and the questions people keep asking you — then proposes five concrete topics, each with a one-line angle and the evidence behind it.

Why it works: The blank page is the bottleneck for most builders who want to write or post regularly. A list of ideas grounded in what your audience already asked about removes it.

How to build it: Gather three inputs: your top posts by engagement, the recurring questions in your comments or inbox, and one or two trending topics in your field. Ask the model to connect them: "which audience question matches which of my top-performing topics, and what angle hasn't been covered yet?" The output is a shortlist, not a content calendar. You pick one and write it yourself.

Pitfall: Don't let it generate the article. The moment the content is AI-written end to end, it reads like everything else. The agent's job is ideas and research, not authorship.

What it does: You give it a question — "what changed in the AI coding tools market this month?" — and three small agents handle it: one plans the research, one gathers sources, one writes up the findings with citations. You review the final memo.

Why it works: One model doing everything in a single pass tends to skim. Splitting the work into planner, researcher and writer produces noticeably better depth, because each step has a narrow job and its own output to check.

How to build it: This is the most ambitious project on the list, but the pattern is simple:

Run it as three sequential model calls, not a fancy framework. Log every intermediate output so you can see where it went wrong. The first version will be rough — the planner will ask the wrong sub-questions. Fix the planner prompt, not the architecture.

Pitfall: Unchecked output. An agent team that runs unattended and publishes its own memo is a misinformation machine with extra steps. The human review is part of the system, not an optional extra.

Don't build all five. Pick the one that matches a task you already hate doing daily — for most people that's the morning brief or the inbox triage — and build the smallest version that works. A script that runs once, manually, and saves you ten minutes is a success. You can automate it later.

The pattern behind all five is the same: a narrow job, a human in the loop at the one step that matters, and no pretence that the AI is autonomous. Small automations, kept honest, compound. Grand agent systems, left unchecked, mostly compound your inbox.

#9687. How an AI assistant can buy a travel eSIM: a look at doctorSIM's public MCP server

If you have built an agent that plans trips, the last step is usually where it stalls. The assistant can pick a destination and compare options, then it has to hand the user a link and hope. We run doctorSIM, an online store for travel eSIMs, prepaid top-ups and digital gift cards, and we publish a remote MCP server so an assistant can go further: read the live catalog, check a phone number, and create an order. This post walks through what the server does and how the calls fit together.

The endpoint is https://api.doctorsim.com/mcp. It speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP, so any client that supports remote servers can connect without a local process. For guest checkout it needs no API key and no headers. OAuth 2.0 exists for PRO accounts that want to pay from prepaid credit, but you can ignore it for the flow below.

The server exposes 23 tools. They cover eSIM destinations and plans, carrier lookup, operator rates, gift card brands, orders and, for linked accounts, balance and webhooks. Prices are never stored in the model's memory or in your prompt: the assistant reads them from the catalog in the same conversation.

The eSIM flow needs no phone number. It goes in five calls:

Between steps 2 and 3 the assistant should repeat the choice to the user: destination, plan and currency. Creating an order is the one step worth a pause.

The top-up flow starts from a phone number in E.164 format, the + followed by country code and number.

A wrong digit sends credit to a stranger, so the assistant should read the number back before the last call. If the carrier lookup fails, get_countries and get_operators let the user pick the operator by hand. When a service has several types, get_operator_service_types shows which operator id applies to which type.

We could have let the assistant take card details. We did not, on purpose. A guest order returns a link on doctorsim.com, the user opens it, enters an email and pays on our checkout. The product is sent to that email after payment.

That keeps card data out of the chat, the model's context and your logs, and the user gets a normal checkout. The link expires after six hours; if the user comes back later, create the order again from the same selection.

One practical rule follows from this. For guest orders, the assistant should not promise a QR code in the conversation. It arrives by email. The status call is there so the assistant can answer "did it go through?" without guessing.

Most MCP clients accept a block like this one. Field names differ a little between clients, so check your client's documentation for the exact key:

Leave headers empty. In clients that ask for an OAuth client ID and secret, leave both blank for guest use.

Then try a prompt such as "I'm going to Japan for ten days, find me an eSIM with plenty of data". A well-behaved assistant will call get_esim_destinations, then get_esim_plans, show a short list and wait for your choice before creating anything.

The agent documentation is at https://www.doctorsim.com/en/developers-agents.html and the MCP guide is at https://www.doctorsim.com/api-docs/mcp.html. If you want to see the customer side of the product, the eSIM catalog is at https://www.doctorsim.com/en/esim/.

If your client hits a case we did not describe here, tell us through the contact page.

#9686. How to Build an MCP Server That Checks npm Packages Before AI Installs Them

Senior Technical Writer | Software Developer

Senior Technical Writer | Software Developer

Senior Technical Writer | Software Developer

Build a remote MCP server on Cloudflare Workers with the 2026-07-28 spec and TypeScript SDK v2. It checks npm packages for typos, deprecation and known vulnerabilities before your AI installs them.

AI coding assistants are good at writing npm install lines. They're less good at knowing whether the package in that line is real, abandoned, or a trap.

I wanted my assistant to check before it suggests anything. So I built a small MCP server for it: two tools, running on Cloudflare Workers, using the new stateless MCP spec from July 2026. It's free to host and needs no API keys.

This post walks through the build. It also covers the parts that surprised me, and a few of them changed how the tools work.

The server is called pkgscout. It exposes two tools:

Both tools only read public data from the npm registry. That keeps the server simple, and it means the free Workers plan is enough.

Until this year, a remote MCP server kept a session open with each client. The client sent an initialize request, the server returned an Mcp-Session-Id, and every request after that had to reach a server that remembered the session. On a platform like Workers, where any request can land on any instance, that was awkward.

The 2026-07-28 spec removes that handshake. Each request carries what the server needs, so any instance can answer it. For a Worker, that's the natural model. You build a fresh server for each request, answer it, and throw it away.

SDK v2 is built around this. It also splits the old single @modelcontextprotocol/sdk package into separate client and server packages, so older tutorials won't match what you see when you install it.

The Wrangler config is short. Turning on observability gives you logs in the Cloudflare dashboard without any extra setup.

One thing I expected to fight with and didn't: JSON Schema validation on Workers. Validators that compile schemas with eval don't run there. SDK v2 checks the runtime and uses a Workers-safe validator automatically, so there was nothing to configure.

All the data comes from registry.npmjs.org. I put the registry calls in their own file, src/registry.ts, and the MCP code just calls those functions.

My first version fetched the full package document (the "packument") to get everything in one request. That works for small packages. For a big one, it's a different story. When I checked, the typescript packument was about 16 MB, because it lists every version ever published. Its /latest manifest was under 5 KB.

That matters on Workers. The free plan gives each request 10 ms of CPU time. Parsing megabytes of JSON for one lookup is a good way to blow through that.

So the server asks for //latest instead. Every registry call goes through one small helper:

The cf.cacheTtl option is a nice Workers detail. Cloudflare caches the registry response at the edge, so when the model asks about zod three times in one conversation, the repeat calls can be answered from cache instead of going back to npm.

The manifest doesn't include download counts. The registry's search endpoint does, so I called /-/v1/search?text= and picked the hit with the matching name.

That worked for hono. It didn't work for request, the old HTTP client. I asked search for request and got retry-request, teeny-request, @types/request and 22 others. The request package itself wasn't in the top 25 results.

I tried two more deprecated packages, querystring and left-pad. Neither showed up in its own top 25 either. Search clearly ranks deprecated packages low. That's sensible for humans browsing npm. It's bad for a tool whose job is to tell the model "this package is deprecated."

The fix was to get downloads from npm's downloads API and keep search as a fallback:

With that change, request came back with its deprecation notice and about 14 million downloads last week. Deprecated since 2020, and still one of the most downloaded packages on npm. That's exactly the kind of package a model will keep suggesting.

This is the part that made the project worth writing about.

When a package doesn't exist, the most useful thing the tool can do is point at the package the model probably meant. My first attempt passed the misspelled name to npm search and returned the top five results.

I tested it with reqeusts, a plausible typo for requests. Search returned simple-server-request, clientside-api-request, nifty-guard, @yof/cli and @tutorbot/api-client. None of them had more than 200 weekly downloads, and none had anything to do with HTTP requests.

That's worse than returning nothing. A model reading "similar packages" will happily suggest one of them.

So I stopped asking search and generated the typos myself. Most misspellings are two letters swapped or one letter dropped, so the server builds those variants and checks which ones exist:

The cap matters. The Workers free plan allows 50 outbound fetches per request. Without a limit, a long package name would generate enough variants to hit it.

With this change, reqeusts returned three real packages: requests, reqests and reqeust. I looked them up one by one, and none of them is what you want.

Three typo neighbours, three different traps. Returning bare names wasn't enough, so each suggestion now comes with the same warnings as a normal lookup:

I could have returned raw fields and let the model work it out. But "version": "0.0.1-security" only means something if you already know npm's conventions. "Do not install" leaves nothing to interpret.

Here's what inspect_package returns for reqeusts now (trimmed):

The second tool uses the endpoint npm audit talks to. You POST a map of package names to versions, and it returns matching advisories:

The catch is that it wants exact versions. If you send ^4.17.0, you won't get a useful answer. Models love sending ranges, because that's what they see in package.json files. So the input schema rejects anything that doesn't start with a real version number:

When validation fails, the SDK sends the message back to the model as a tool error instead of crashing the request. The model sees packages.0.version: Use an exact version and can fix its own call.

Testing lodash@4.17.15 returned five advisories, three of them rated high. Then I tried 4.17.21, the version a lot of us remember as "the fixed one." It still matches two advisories: a high-severity code injection in _.template and a prototype pollution bug in _.unset. The current release is 4.18.1.

That's a good example of why this tool is useful. A model trained on older code will confidently suggest 4.17.21 as the safe version.

With the registry code done, the MCP part is short. Each tool gets a name, a description written for the model, a schema, and a handler:

createMcpHandler takes a factory function, not a server. It calls buildServer() for each request, which is the whole idea of the new spec. Nothing is kept between requests, so it doesn't matter which Cloudflare instance answers.

It also handles older clients. By default, requests that use the 2025 protocol are served statelessly too, so a client that hasn't updated yet still works.

For auth I used a single bearer token stored as a Worker secret. safeEqual (in the repo, about ten lines) hashes both values and compares the hashes, so the check takes the same time whether the token is close or completely wrong. A shared token is fine for a personal server. If you plan to share yours, the new spec's OAuth rules are the next step.

To test without wiring up a whole AI client, I wrote a short script with the v2 client package:

That versionNegotiation line cost me some time. Without it, the v2 client still speaks the 2025 protocol. Everything worked, so nothing looked wrong. I only noticed because I logged which protocol each request used and every one said legacy. Setting mode: "auto" makes the client try the 2026 protocol first.

You can see the difference in the wrangler dev output. With the old protocol, the client opens with a handshake and a GET /mcp that the server rejects with a 405. With the new one, it's just a series of POST /mcp requests, each one complete on its own.

If you'd rather click than script, MCP Inspector v2 can talk the new protocol too. Start it with --protocol-era modern and it shows the negotiated version right on the connection card:

That printf %s is there for a reason. The first time, I pasted the token into the secrets screen in the dashboard and every request came back 401. The value the Worker stored didn't match the one in my terminal, most likely because of a stray character from the paste. Piping it from the same shell variable your client uses rules that out. A quick check before you wire up a client:

A 401 means the token is wrong. A 415 means auth passed and the server just wants a real MCP request.

Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://pkgscout..workers.dev. Each tool call writes one JSON log line with the tool name, the outcome and how long it took, and you can read them under Observability in the Cloudflare dashboard.

Then ask for something that needs a package. A good test is adding lodash@4.17.21 to a small Node script, since that's the version a lot of older code pins. This is the check the assistant should run first, done by hand in MCP Inspector:

The MCP part of this project was the easy part. Most of the work went into the data: noticing that search hides deprecated packages, that typo suggestions can point at malicious ones, and that the "safe" lodash version isn't safe anymore. That's where a tool like this earns its place in your editor.

The code is on GitHub: https://github.com/tarunsinghofficial/pkgscout. If you try it with a misspelling that slips past it, I'd like to hear about it.

#9685. Three filters, cheap to expensive: how a duplicate finder avoids hashing your whole disk

Every duplicate file finder starts with the same obvious plan: hash every file, group by digest. It is correct, it is simple, and on a real drive it is unusable.

Here is the naive baseline, measured on a 1.09 GB working folder with 877 files:

21 seconds for one gigabyte. A 500 GB drive is three hours, and that is before you count the USB drive that spins down every 30 seconds.

The fix is not a faster hash. SHA-256 is already fast enough — the CPU is not the bottleneck, the disk is. The fix is not reading the bytes at all for the files that cannot possibly be duplicates.

os.stat gives you the size without opening the file. Two files with different sizes are not duplicates, full stop. This filter costs one syscall per file and eliminates the majority of a normal folder.

Only buckets with more than one member survive. On a typical disk that is a small fraction of the file count — photos, videos, and documents almost all have unique sizes.

Files that share a size are the only candidates left. For those, read 4 KB and hash that.

4 KB is not a magic number. It is the point where the cost of the read is negligible compared to opening the file at all, and where formats diverge: JPEG headers, ZIP local headers, MP4 ftyp boxes, and Office files all differ within the first few hundred bytes. Two files that agree on both size and first 4 KB are either duplicates or deliberately constructed to look like them.

Whatever is still standing gets read end to end and hashed properly.

The point of this stage is not speed. It is that this is the only stage allowed to decide a file gets deleted, and it uses a cryptographic digest, not CRC32, not a size match, not a filename pattern. Duplicate cleaners get one-star reviews for exactly one reason: they deleted something that was not a duplicate.

Same folder, same machine, three filters instead of one:

2.1x on 1.09 GB. That number is unimpressive, and it is worth being honest about why: this folder is small and it is full of build artefacts that genuinely collide on size. The ratio is not a constant — it is a function of how much of your disk is unique. On a photo library where every file is a different size, filter 1 alone removes almost everything and the speedup is an order of magnitude. On a folder of copied installers it approaches 1x, because most of the data really is duplicate and really does have to be read.

The metric that matters is not files hashed. It is bytes read, and filters 1 and 2 exist to make that number small.

Hard links. st_nlink > 1 means several names point at one inode. They are not duplicates — deleting either name frees nothing, because the data is still referenced. A finder that reports them as duplicates and "cleans" them gives the user a fake number and zero reclaimed space.

Long paths. MAX_PATH is 260 characters and open() fails past it. Prefixing with \\?\ bypasses the limit, but only for absolute paths, and only on Windows:

The 240 threshold, not 260, leaves room for the prefix itself and for the path separator that gets appended.

Four stages, about 40 lines of logic, and the expensive one runs on a third of the files or fewer. The same shape works for photo libraries, backups, and the Downloads folder everyone has been meaning to clean since 2019.

FileDedupe is a Windows duplicate file finder that uses this pipeline. Free on the Microsoft Store. Code excerpts above are from the shipping scanner.

#9684. Your Development Partner Writes Code With AI. What Changes for You?

An AI tool can suggest a change to an existing product. The harder part for a client is seeing which product rules the team gave it, where the tool must stop, and who owns the released result

A service manager asks for a change to the message customers receive when an appointment is rescheduled. The new time should appear immediately. The development partner says it will use AI to prepare the change. That sounds like a detail of the workflow until someone asks what happens to the provider’s calendar, an earlier confirmation, or a reschedule made manually by an operator.

This is a hypothetical service, not a Qtim client story. It makes a common gap visible: a tool may produce a plausible patch from the information it can see, while the actual product also depends on rules in operations, settings, integrations, and decisions made long before this request. The client does not need to write instructions for a coding agent. The client does need to know how the team turns its understanding of the product into a bounded task, and who resolves a gap in that understanding.

An engineer who has worked on a service for months may remember that an appointment update affects provider availability and the support queue. An AI coding tool has no such memory by default. It works from the files, descriptions, examples, and instructions made available to it. Someone decides which of those materials are relevant and current, and which actions the tool may take.

That decision is additional work specific to AI-assisted development. The team has to select context for the tool rather than merely gather information for its own understanding. It has to reconcile conflicting sources, mark missing rules, and set limits on access and changes. Handing over a large repository is not equivalent to explaining the business process. An old instruction can look as authoritative as a current rule when the tool has no reason to tell them apart.

In a 2025 study, Jiang and Nam examined developer-written rule files in 401 open-source repositories. The files covered project information, team conventions, guidelines, examples, and directions written for language models. This is evidence about the kinds of context developers choose to record. The study did not test whether adding such a file improved task success. Its sample of open-source repositories also cannot stand in for every commercial product.

The authors of CAFE(S) offered a useful framework in September 2026: context should be clear, actionable, faithful to the project, economical, and secure. It is a conceptual framework, not a measured promise of faster delivery. For a client, the practical question is more direct: what verified information did the team use to frame the task for its AI tool, and who will notice when that information is incomplete?

Consider the proposed message again. “Tell the customer the new time” says nothing about a confirmation already sent, a provider who is no longer available, or a change entered by an operator. Some rules may be in the application. Others may sit in configuration or in a support procedure. A generated change may fit the visible code and still conflict with how the service actually runs.

The team should establish the relevant slice of the product before it asks the tool to work on it. When is the appointment officially rescheduled? Who can trigger the change? Where is the time stored? Which notifications already go out? What happens when an operator intervenes? These questions also matter in development without AI. AI adds a distinct handoff: the team must choose verified answers for the tool, identify unanswered questions, and prevent a plausible guess from becoming product policy.

That handoff can be made visible without showing the client prompts or code. For one change, a short working agreement can cover four things:

Context: the situations in which an appointment changes and the current operations affected by the message.

Boundary: the messages and statuses the team may change, and the behaviors it must preserve.

Owner: the person who resolves a disputed rule and approves a change to it.

Evidence of completion: the customer, provider, and operator scenarios that should work after release.

The business owner confirms the operational rules and exceptions. The development partner translates them into a workable assignment, controls the tool’s scope, and checks the result in the product. This is relevant when developing an existing product. Qtim’s service page describes work on existing products; it is not evidence that the team used AI on a particular client project.

Suppose an operator can reschedule an appointment manually, but the system does not store a reason. Should the customer receive an explanation? A neighboring file may suggest one answer, while the real support procedure suggests another. The coding tool cannot settle a business rule by imitating surrounding code. A responsible team pauses the change, asks the process owner, and resumes once the rule is clear.

The pause may feel slow when a tool can produce several implementation options in minutes. It prevents the team from delivering a neatly assembled message that breaks the actual customer journey. The difference appears before code review: the team separates confirmed conditions from guesses when constructing the AI task. It also decides what the tool can access. CAFE(S) treats security as part of context quality. The right data and access limits depend on the product and the tool, but the responsibility for setting them must belong to named people.

There is a reasonable objection here: experienced developers also need context, and they can make the same mistake. True. AI does not create the need to understand a product. It creates another place where understanding can be lost or distorted. A human engineer may ask a colleague about an ambiguous rule; the tool may proceed from an incomplete input and offer a confident-looking answer. The team therefore needs a deliberate step to prepare and constrain what the tool sees, plus a clear rule for stopping when the answer is missing.

The client expects the agreed change to work across the relevant scenarios and to remain supportable. The team must inspect its proposed solution, explain why it fits the product, and release it through its normal process. The detailed mechanics of code review are a separate subject. Here the issue is who stands behind the decision to use a particular change.

A 2025 IBM study surveyed two cohorts of developers, 669 people in total, and ran 15 unmoderated usability tests of an internal coding assistant. The authors discuss ownership and responsibility for generated code. Those are developer experiences inside IBM, not contract terms for another company. They support asking who owns the output; they do not supply the answer for any specific engagement.

Nor does the method of writing code settle its future quality. A peer-reviewed 2026 experiment involved 151 participants, about 95% professional developers. In its second phase, new participants extended code created with or without AI assistance. The study found no systematic difference in the time or quality of that subsequent work within its tasks. The work used one Java web application and was conducted in late 2024, before newer coding-agent workflows became common. It does not establish that all AI-assisted code is harmless, or that it is inherently difficult to maintain. A client still needs the team to validate the particular change it releases.

The evidence on speed also depends on what is measured. Three field experiments reported by Microsoft Research in 2025 found more completed tasks among developers who had access to a code-completion assistant. In an earlier randomized study, METR found that experienced open-source contributors took longer on familiar repository tasks when AI tools were allowed. METR’s 2026 update warns that selection effects made its later estimates difficult to interpret.

These studies used different people, tools, settings, and outcome measures. Neither counts the time needed to learn the appointment service’s operating rules, prepare reliable context, resolve exceptions, validate the change, and release it. A partner can use AI in some parts of the work. A deadline or price for this product still needs to be based on the full scope and its known uncertainties. A claim that “AI makes it cheaper” supplies neither.

The appointment message gives the parties a manageable starting point. Agree when a reschedule is complete, which messages are in scope, who resolves disputed cases, and what the customer, provider, and operator should observe afterward. Then the team can choose how to use AI within that agreement. The order matters: a tool cannot responsibly answer questions the product owner has not settled.

Decision rule: assess the partner’s AI workflow through the verified context it prepares, the limits it sets for the tool, and the human who owns the released result. The tool can change how options are produced. It does not take the partner’s responsibility for the product change.

If an existing product needs a defined change, the our team can discuss the affected area and its constraints before the implementation is estimated.

#9683. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9681. Sinking Production with Silent Config Drifts: Building a Fail-Fast Guardrail for Giant YAML/JSON Setups

Configuration drift is one of the quietest killers in distributed backend architectures. When configuration files scale to thousands of lines across heterogeneous staging and production environments, subtle omissions—a missing required field, an unquoted integer interpreted as a string, or a misplaced nested mapping—often bypass basic line linters and stay undetected until deployment runtime.

To eliminate this vulnerability before services touch orchestration clusters, we engineered a deterministic, schema-enforcing validation CLI. Designed to intercept misconfigurations within CI/CD pipelines, this tool parses multi-format configuration files (YAML/JSON) and evaluates them against strict Pydantic v2 schemas.

Here is an architectural deep dive into the implementation, the post-mortem of a failure encountered in QA testing, the complete codebase, and lessons learned on execution environment guarantees.

The CLI utility takes a path to a configuration file as an argument, selects an optimized parsing strategy based on the file extension (YAML or JSON), and feeds the resulting raw data structure into a Pydantic v2 schema for strict structural and type validation.

During execution in the QA verification pipeline, the script failed immediately upon invocation with the following fatal traceback:

This termination was triggered by our defensive import guards placed at the head of the script:

The issue was not a code defect, logic regression, or syntax incompatibility. The underlying problem was an unmanaged environment contract: external dependencies (orjson, PyYAML, and pydantic) were not codified, pinned, or automatically provisioned in the runner container prior to test execution.

While the script's defensive guards fulfilled their purpose—terminating the process safely with an informative error message (exit(1)) rather than crashing on an unhandled NameError or nested traceback downstack—dependency resolution had been treated as an implicit external prerequisite rather than an explicit build artifact. In automated headless environments, code-level robustness cannot compensate for missing environment orchestration.

Below is the complete standalone script engineered for type safety, granular error reporting, and defensive execution:

💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want).

Analyzing this breakdown yields critical engineering patterns for internal developer tooling and platform validation:

A script with exhaustive defensive guards and rigorous typing remains non-operational if execution environments do not guarantee declared dependencies. Internal CLI tools must never rely on implicit system-level packages. Dependency manifests (pyproject.toml with pip-tools or Poetry/uv locks) and reproducible container runners must be treated with the same engineering rigor as production microservices.

Choosing orjson provides exceptional throughput for high-volume serialization workloads, but it introduces compiled C/Rust binary dependencies that can complicate minimal environments (e.g., Alpine-based containers or scratch images lacking musl wheels). When building lightweight validation utilities, architects must evaluate whether standard library modules (such as built-in json) suffice, or bundle tools via self-contained distribution mechanisms (like shiv or pex).

Automated pipelines must not assume pre-warmed runners. Smoke testing must begin with an ephemeral, clean-room environment where dependency resolution, installation, and end-to-end schema validation are evaluated from scratch. Ensuring that bootstrapping succeeds without cached artifacts is the only way to avoid breaking continuous deployment gates.

#9679. I built Aegis — a personal cyber defense platform that checks links, emails, files and passwords before they hurt you

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at github.com

Most people don't get hacked by nation-state attacks. They get hacked by a fake link in a text message, a convincing "verify your account" email, a malware attachment disguised as an invoice, or a password that already leaked in someone else's data breach.

So I built Aegis — one place where a non-technical person can check each of those things before it hurts them, built to the same security standard it checks for.

🔗 Live demo: https://aegis-cyber-defense-platform.onrender.com (free hosting — first load after idle can take ~ a minute) 💻 Code: https://github.com/Manoj-2424150118/aegis-cyber-defense-platform

Smart Scan is the front door: paste anything — a link, an email, a suspicious message — and Aegis detects what it is and routes it to the right analyser automatically.

Underneath are 10 tools, each answering a question a worried user actually asks:

Every finding in every report ends with a Suggested Fix — concrete next steps written for the person holding the report. A test enforces that no finding can ship without one. A report should end the problem, not just name it.

Since v2.0, a detection-engine "Signal" layer sits across the analysers, and public Trends show what people are actually checking.

A security tool has to survive its own audit:

186 automated tests, all passing, with CI and CodeQL green on every push. The canonical reference scores never drift between releases: the reference phishing link scores 85, the phishing email 100, the disguised program 40 — in every battery, on every version. A scripted QA battery (functional checks, attack suite, fuzzing, load) runs in a sandbox before deployment and against the live site after it.

FastAPI (Python) back end, React + TypeScript front end, single Docker container, Neon Postgres for storage (accounts and vault items survive redeploys — proven by test).

I'm Manoj Kumar Sharma, a cybersecurity & software professional (MCA, Manipal University Jaipur) based in Jaipur, India. I also run Scam Decoded, where I break down real Indian scams in short videos.

If you try Aegis, I'd genuinely like to hear what it got right — and what it missed.

#9678. MatterSeek AI: A Guide to Reverse Materials Design and Property Prediction

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

MatterSeek-New-Materials-Reverse-Design is presented as the reverse-design offering in Yuyao Technology’s MatterSeek materials-prediction platform. It targets inorganic and organic materials R&D: users specify desired properties and elemental constraints, and the service proposes compositions, structures, and processing parameters. The supplied maintainer is YuyaoTechnology. The README describes MatterSeek as beta and recommends using predictions to prioritize experiments, followed by offline validation.

Use it to screen candidate materials against target properties, explore composition and element constraints, and generate ranked candidates for multi-objective design. It is also described for forward property prediction from composition formulas or other supported inputs, and for proposing synthesis windows such as sintering or annealing parameters. The stated coverage spans 17 materials domains, including superconductivity, catalysis, optics, mechanics, thermoelectrics, and crystal structure.

The README says predictions should support experiment prioritization, not replace final characterization; it recommends offline validation before scale-up, especially for critical or regulated applications. Coverage is bounded by the 17 domains and 192 target properties, and emerging combinations or properties outside that taxonomy may require extension through new experiments. The README reports held-out experimental evaluation within the provider’s own corpus but supplies no numerical benchmark results or public peer comparison. It describes the platform as beta.

The supplied related-model entries do not establish a like-for-like materials-design comparison, so no capability, quality, speed, or cost ranking is supported. The only supplied internal alternative link is MatterSeek, which appears to refer to the broader MatterSeek offering rather than a documented independent alternative. The README’s benchmark note says no public benchmark or peer model covers its exact set of 192 performance variables.

The README describes a proprietary hierarchical neural network (HNN): a shared backbone learns cross-domain representations from 1,035 material descriptors, with 192 expert sub-models grouped under 17 domains. It says physics-informed regularization applies symmetry, conservation-law, and thermodynamic constraints as soft penalties. Training is described as two stages: self-supervised masked-fingerprint or structure reconstruction on composition–structure–property records, followed by domain fine-tuning with physics-informed loss and active-learning feedback. The stated data comprises several million records, predominantly proprietary high-throughput experimental measurements and curated literature values, with structural data supplemented by DFT. No parameter count, context length, downloadable weight format, hardware requirement, or numerical performance result is supplied. The model card’s text-generation pipeline tag does not provide a documented local inference interface for this materials-design service.

Documented inputs include natural-language chemistry instructions, target property metrics, elemental constraints, and composition formulas. The interface is described as supporting element selection through an interactive periodic table and filtering by composition range. No exact schema, units, or API request format is provided.

The README describes predicted properties with uncertainty bounds, recommended compositions including Pareto-front candidates, crystal structures, processing parameters such as sintering or annealing windows, and ranked experiment proposals. Results are presented with multidimensional visualization. The source does not specify a machine-readable output schema.

Q: What is MatterSeek-New-Materials-Reverse-Design for?

A: It is presented as a materials reverse-design service that proposes candidate compositions, structures, and processing conditions from target properties and constraints. It also supports forward property prediction according to the README.

A: The README describes 17 domains and 192 target-property sub-models, including superconductivity, catalysis, optics, mechanics, thermoelectrics, and crystal structure. It says coverage is bounded by the current taxonomy.

A: Supported input types described in the README are natural-language chemistry instructions, property targets, elemental constraints, and composition formulas. The interface also describes selecting elements and filtering composition ranges.

A: Described results include predicted properties with uncertainty bounds, candidate compositions, crystal structures, processing windows, and ranked experiment proposals. The README also mentions Pareto-front candidates for multi-objective design.

Q: Can its predictions replace laboratory validation?

A: No. The README recommends using predictions to prioritize experiments and says they should not substitute for final characterization; it advises offline validation before scale-up.

Q: Is there a public benchmark or peer comparison?

A: The README says evaluation uses held-out experimental test sets split by material family within the provider’s corpus. It reports no public benchmark or peer comparison for the exact set of 192 performance variables.

A: No reliable local inference example or API schema is supplied. The README describes an interactive product workflow, but does not provide code for loading or calling model weights.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called MatterSeek-New-Materials-Reverse-Design maintained by YuyaoTechnology. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

#9677. I made a React component that opens and edits DOCX / XLSX / PPTX in the browser. 300k-row sheet in ~300ms, no server, MIT

Why: I needed "customer uploads an XLSX, fix a few cells, save it back" inside a React app. OnlyOffice / Collabora mean running a document server in Docker and an iframe talking to it, and a big sheet still sits on a spinner while the server converts it. docx-preview / SheetJS + a grid are view-only or block the main thread on a 20 MB file. Nothing in between, so I built it.

src takes File / Blob / ArrayBuffer / URL. CSS is auto-injected, the container just needs a height. There's also a useDocument hook if you want to render your own UI, a vanilla mount(), an web component, and a single script build.

ZIP read lazily, HTTP Range requests from a URL, so first rows show before the file finishes downloading

Streaming XML parser in a Web Worker, main thread only gets rows / paragraphs / slides as they arrive

Only visible pages, cells, slides are in the DOM

Save patches the original file instead of re-exporting it, so anything the engine doesn't understand is kept byte for byte

Bundle (gzip): main ~93 KB, worker ~155 KB (loads off the main thread), collab +17 KB optional. The standalone script with React bundled is ~307 KB.

Editing: DOCX text / styles / lists / images / tables, XLSX cells / formulas (134 functions) / formats / rows / columns / sheets, PPTX text / shapes / images / slides. Google Docs style toolbar. Optional real-time collab with cursors; that's the only part needing a backend (a small WebSocket hub, Bun script included).

Not there yet: XLSX charts / pivots / conditional formatting editing, DOCX headers / footers read-only, no PPTX animations. It needs the DOM and a Worker, so in Next.js use a client component / dynamic import with ssr: false.

Fair warning: it's a few days old and a lot of it was written with Claude Code, with me doing architecture, review and the bug hunting on real files. If you throw a file at it and it breaks, open an issue with the file, that's the fastest way it gets fixed.

Repo: https://github.com/p10node/office-engine

Demo (drag your own file in): https://p10node.github.io/office-engine/demo/

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at frontendfacile.it

Prezzi più bassi, agent swarm da 1.000 istanze, generazione di OS e 3D in Three.js: segnali pratici di un salto di qualità nei modelli “coding-first”.

Negli ultimi mesi ci siamo abituati a release incrementali: piccoli miglioramenti di qualità, qualche ottimizzazione di costo, nuove policy. Con Fable/Mythos 5.2, però, il messaggio implicito è diverso: non è solo “più bravo a scrivere snippet”, ma sembra pensato per reggere carichi lunghi, complessi e multi-step — quelli che assomigliano di più al lavoro reale.

Prima di entrare nelle demo, due definizioni utili per orientarsi.

Per chi sviluppa prodotti web, la differenza pratica è soprattutto questa: quanto puoi spingere in autonomia su certe richieste (automazione aggressiva, ricerca su exploit, ecc.) e quanto devi rimanere in un perimetro più controllato.

Il nuovo listino dichiarato scende a $8 in / $40 out, in calo rispetto alla generazione precedente.

Nota importante: viene comunque consigliato di usare un modello “generalista” (tipo Opus) per la maggior parte dei task, e passare a Fable solo quando serve davvero. Tradotto in logica da team:

Questa impostazione è molto simile a come si gestiscono tier di infrastruttura: non metti il cluster più costoso dietro ogni endpoint.

La parte davvero interessante è l’uso di molti sub-agenti (si parla di uno swarm nell’ordine delle 1.000 istanze) su tempi lunghi. Questo cambia il tipo di problemi che diventano affrontabili:

Per un frontend engineer questo è rilevante perché porta a un paradigma in cui il modello non è un copilota, ma un sistema di build vivente: genera, testa, corregge e integra.

Uno dei test più estremi: partire da una cartella vuota e arrivare a un OS completo con kernel/driver, avviabile su hardware reale.

Al di là dell’effetto wow, l’implicazione pratica è chiara: se un modello può mantenere coerenza su un progetto “intero” di questo tipo, allora può farlo anche su:

In altre parole: si riduce il gap tra “ti scrivo una funzione” e “ti porto il progetto da A a B senza rompere tutto”.

Un altro benchmark notevole riguarda la produzione di una dimostrazione verificabile (in stile formal verification). Il dato interessante non è la matematica in sé, ma che un processo così rigido costringe il sistema a:

Per chi fa frontend, è un proxy utile: un modello che regge vincoli formali tende ad essere più affidabile anche quando deve rispettare:

Si cita la progettazione di dispositivi (hub voice assistant, speakerphone USB, “virtual pet” handheld) a partire da un prompt breve.

Per un frontend dev, non è tanto “ok, progetta circuiti”, quanto:

Se lavori su dashboard per device o companion app, questa convergenza conta.

I benchmark comparativi sono tanti e spesso autoreferenziali. In ambito frontend, quello che conta è: riesce a generare esperienze interattive solide, leggibili e manutenibili?

Un test emblematico è chiedere un 3D realistico interattivo in Three.js.

Qui il salto è nel come: invece di importare un asset preconfezionato, il modello costruisce l’animale proceduralmente (approccio tipo signed distance fields), lo mesha, lo riga a uno scheletro e lo anima.

In più, emerge un comportamento che vale oro nella pratica: autovalutazione + iterazione. Il sistema riconosce difetti visivi (proporzioni, criniera, coda, ecc.) e rientra in ciclo di correzione.

È esattamente il tipo di loop che serve quando lavori su:

Se queste capacità reggono anche fuori dalle demo, si delineano tre implicazioni molto concrete.

I risultati migliori arrivano quando tratti il modello come un team member a cui dai:

Con prezzi ancora non banali, la strategia realistica è:

Fable/Mythos 5.2 non colpisce tanto per la singola feature, ma per un pattern: resistenza su task lunghi, capacità di orchestrazione multi-agente e iterazione qualitativa su output complessi (fino a esperienze 3D interattive in browser).

Per chi fa frontend, il takeaway è pratico: i modelli stanno diventando abbastanza solidi da essere usati non solo per generare codice, ma per portare avanti interi filoni di lavoro—con un livello di controllo che dipende sempre più da come imposti specifiche, verifiche e pipeline.

Se oggi investissi tempo su una sola cosa, non sarebbe “imparare il prompt perfetto”, ma costruire un workflow ripetibile: strumenti, test, budget prestazionali e criteri di qualità che trasformano un output generato in qualcosa che puoi mantenere in produzione.

#9675. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. If you’re only in charge of dessert this year and want to flex a little, this recipe is an impressive (and tasty!) way to do so.

Shop the recipe: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

Mash-up pies are an easy way to please your guests without making multiple pies. This recipe has the best of both worlds: a smooth layer of spiced pumpkin custard plus a rich pecan topping. It’s best made a day ahead so that the flavors can settle, plus there’s one less dish to worry about on Thanksgiving Day.

Shop the recipe: Adjustable Pie Crust Shield

Is there anything cuter than a mini Thanksgiving pie? Filled with a pre-cooked, perfectly spiced filling that’s enhanced with tart boiled cider, these bite-sized treats can be topped with a woven lattice or streusel.

This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

Shop the recipe: Pure Almond Extract and Sparkling Sugar

This stunning pumpkin swirl cake is more than just good looks: It also has a soft, plush texture, thanks to cake flour and sour cream, and a deep pumpkin flavor paired with fragrant vanilla. It starts with one base batter that gets flavored two ways, creating two distinct colors for a striking visual contrast when sliced.

For a more traditional dessert, try this pumpkin-y layer cake. It’s moist and slightly dense from the pumpkin purée, with a tangy cream cheese frosting and sticky caramel glaze.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

In this unabashedly apple-forward apple cake, there are so many apple slices and so little batter, you’ll wonder how (and if) it will hold together. But never fear: As the batter rises in the oven, it knits those slices together to create a tender cake that’s almost creamy and custardy due to the abundance of fruit.

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Pure Almond Extract

The pumpkin and pumpkin-friendly spices (cloves, cinnamon, allspice) in this cake meld surprisingly well with the chocolate chips studded throughout. This dark, moist Bundt cake is rich enough to serve unfrosted, and it's just the ticket when you want to serve a dessert that's substantial, yet not too sweet, to finish your Thanksgiving meal. And it keeps well for days, so you can bake it early in the week to help prep ahead.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

This golden cake is rich, moist, and subtly spiced to complement, rather than overshadow, the natural flavor of sweet potatoes. It also includes a crunchy pecan crust on both the top and bottom, along with a touch of maple syrup in the cake for sweetness. If you’re not a fan of pie, this sweet potato cake just may be the perfect Thanksgiving dessert.

Get the recipe: Pecan-Crusted Sweet Potato Pound Cake

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Tube Pan

With a hidden swirl of coffee-flavored filling, this stunning cake adds an extra dimension to your holiday table. It’s like a pumpkin spice latte in dessert form — and also secretly whole wheat!

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

Wondering how far ahead you can make your cake? Here's how long cake lasts in the fridge and at room temp.

This cake is an old favorite of our readers, with over 300 five-star reviews. It's a recipe where the whole is definitely more than the sum of the parts: The moist, semi-chunky cake is packed with four cups of apples, then spread with the frosting equivalent of brown sugar fudge. The whole thing comes together by hand in one bowl, so it also fits easily into your Thanksgiving prep.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

Shop the recipe: Apple Pie Spice and Vermont Boiled Cider

Why decide between cheesecake and pie when you can have both? This eye-catching two-toned recipe pairs custardy pumpkin pie with creamy cheesecake for a dessert that will satisfy everyone.

For an all-pumpkin Thanksgiving cheesecake, there’s this classic version, which transforms pumpkin pie into a silky, velvety filling. Because it needs to chill before serving, this cheesecake is an excellent candidate for baking a day ahead of Thanksgiving.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cheesecake with Gingersnap Crust

Shop the recipe: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

We did the testing: This is the best way to keep your cheesecake from cracking.

It’s right there in the name: This is an easy, failproof cheesecake that comes together quickly and bakes up beautifully. You don’t even need a water bath! Top with maple- or bourbon-spiked whipped cream to dress it up for the holiday; details are in the recipe tips at the bottom of our Homemade Whipped Cream recipe.

For a fall-forward cheesecake, turn to this seasonal recipe. The texture of the filling is ultra-smooth and creamy, and the maple flavor is apparent, yet subtle — the secret is natural maple flavor paired with maple syrup. The pecan crust, meanwhile, is a nutty, salty counterbalance to the filling.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

If you’re looking for a celebratory yet unexpected dessert for your table, we recommend this recipe. A heavy pour of Irish whiskey cream liqueur (save some for your after-dinner coffee!) flavors the smooth, light filling, while silky chocolate ganache adorns the top. Oven space at a premium while you prep Thanksgiving dinner? This dessert is no-bake, so you can save some room in the cooking schedule.

With its burnished top and custardy interior, this cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This flourless cake is incredibly rich — like sliceable fudge sauce. A thick icing of chocolate ganache glaze takes it over the top, but if you want something a touch lighter after a heavy Thanksgiving feast, top it instead with a dusting of confectioners’ sugar and a spoonful of barely sweetened whipped cream.

Baker's tip: Make your whipped cream in a Mason jar, especially helpful if you're bringing dessert to someone else's home.

Shop the recipe: Callebaut Semisweet Chocolate Chips

This chocolate pie, with its flaky pastry crust and glistening, ruby-colored cranberry topping, is a non-traditional twist on Thanksgiving flavors. With a semisweet chocolate ganache, nutty whole-grain flour in the crust, and tangy fruit, it delivers a novel and enticing new holiday pie.

This pecan tart recipe is the more lavish, decadent cousin of a classic pecan pie. The pecans are enveloped in a rich, chewy caramel filling, and a blanket of velvety smooth chocolate ganache covers the top of the tart, lending it major candy bar vibes with a touch of sophistication.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Semisweet Chocolate Wafers

This nostalgic pie is the perfect combination of crispy crust, dense chocolatey filling, and ethereal whipped cream. The crust is prebaked, then filled with a generous amount of cooked, cooled chocolate filling. You can customize the chocolate flavor to your taste by using bittersweet, semisweet, milk chocolate, or any combination of these that you like.

Based on chess pie, an old Southern favorite, this pie’s texture hits the sweet spot between cheesecake and custard. As it bakes, it also makes its own crackly chocolate-sugar topping, which yields to the dense, fudgy filling beneath.

Watch as Kye shares 4 tips for failproof pie dough.

For years, bakers asked us for a vegan pumpkin pie recipe: This one’s for you! For this dairy-free pie, sweetened condensed coconut milk takes the place of cream, and a cornstarch slurry acts as an egg-like binder. But worry not: Despite being vegan, it has the fragrant spiced flavor of classic pumpkin pie.

Instead of eggs, this pie relies on cornstarch to bind the gooey filling; coconut cream, meanwhile, stands in for butter. With tons of toasty pecans bound together in a rich, sweet syrup and cradled in a flaky crust, it’s hard to believe this pie is vegan.

Shop the recipe: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Guittard Bittersweet Onyx Chocolate Wafers

How do you make a cream pie without dairy or eggs? The secret is coconut: The pudding-like filling is made with both coconut cream and evaporated coconut milk for a rich texture that’s the perfect balance of set but still soft. The sheer amount of chocolate means that it, and not coconut, is still the predominant flavor in this vegan chocolate pie.

Get the recipe: No-Bake Vegan Chocolate Pie

A cake so easy that you can mix it in its pan, this reliable recipe is also free of dairy or eggs. And you won’t miss them: This simple chocolate cake is dark and moist, with a slightly coarse crumb. If you’re worried about getting overwhelmed with all the cooking and baking Thanksgiving morning, we recommend this stress-free recipe.

Get the recipe: King Arthur’s Original Cake Pan Cake
