A simple dump-and-stir batter bakes up into this sweet and spicy vegan cake, which has a moist, tender crumb from the inclusion of pumpkin purée and vegetable oil. Add raisins, walnuts, or dried cranberries to the batter for additional texture and flavor.

Our secret to capturing fall in a dessert? Fragrant, uber-flavorful pumpkin pie spice.

A flaky pie crust can be difficult to achieve with gluten-free flour, but our Gluten-Free All-Purpose Flour — along with xanthan gum and Instant ClearJel to help with binding and structure — is up to the task. The pumpkin filling, meanwhile, is classic: smooth, mildly sweet, and just spicy enough.

Get the recipe: Chocolate Almond Flour Torte

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Belcolade Bittersweet Chocolate Wafers

This perfectly tender cake — made with our Measure for Measure Flour for a seamless gluten-free baking experience — incorporates cinnamon, ginger, cardamom, allspice, and black pepper to mimic the flavors in a steaming cup of chai. Lightly sweetened with both brown sugar and honey, it's an ideal autumnal dessert.

Get the recipe: Gluten-Free Chai-Spiced Pound Cake

Shop the recipe: Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour

This one-bowl cake belies its simplicity with moist texture and out-of-this-world flavor. The combination of mildly spiced cake, chopped fresh apples, and fudge-like brown sugar frosting is guaranteed to be a hit at the end of your Thanksgiving feast.

#9674. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9673. From HTTP to SSH: Finding a Host-Level Attack Path in OpenPLC v3

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

A software PLC does not need a physical controller sitting inside a cabinet to execute industrial control logic. Its runtime can live entirely on a conventional computer, communicating with other systems through familiar industrial protocols while relying on an ordinary operating system underneath, and that changes the security picture.

When assessing a SoftPLC, it is easy to concentrate on the services it exposes: Modbus TCP, management interfaces, perhaps a programming environment. Yet the control logic has to get onto the machine somehow. It has to be stored, compiled, and loaded into a runtime. The host operating system participates in every one of those operations.

I wanted to investigate what happens when an attacker can reach that layer.

The question guiding this research was simple: could someone modify a SoftPLC's active control logic through its deployment environment, replace the existing program, and execute the altered logic without following the usual management workflow?

I began with Beremiz. That did not go particularly well. After nearly nine hours spent trying to understand its internal architecture and communication mechanisms, I changed targets and moved to OpenPLC v3. Even then, my first approach ran into trouble. I eventually abandoned the management API route, turned my attention to SSH, and spent another long stretch figuring out how to make the entire process work remotely.

The resulting proof of concept replaced the active Structured Text program, compiled the substituted logic, restarted the runtime, and verified the resulting process-image changes through Modbus TCP. This is how I got there.

Beremiz was my original target for this investigation. I wanted to examine whether an attacker could modify a SoftPLC's control logic through its deployment environment and demonstrate the result in an isolated lab.

The difficulty appeared before I could properly reach that question.

Beremiz has a fairly involved architecture. Its IDE-to-runtime communication relies on an Embedded Remote Procedure Call (eRPC) subsystem and custom target connectors. Understanding that communication path became a substantial undertaking in itself. The transport and framing mechanisms were not especially convenient to inspect or reproduce manually.

Its deployment workflow also introduced more friction than I wanted for this particular experiment. I was aiming for lightweight, script-driven testing. Instead, I found myself trying to understand the machinery connecting the IDE, target, and runtime before I could meaningfully investigate the control-logic execution path. Nearly nine hours went into that effort.

Eventually, I decided to stop and change targets. I wasn't getting the evidence I wanted, and continuing to reverse-engineer the deployment infrastructure would have consumed even more time. I moved to OpenPLC v3.

OpenPLC v3 offered a more accessible environment for the investigation. Its management application, project storage, compilation process, and runtime gave me several concrete components to examine.

I provisioned an isolated Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machine using Multipass. The machine was deliberately modest: two virtual CPUs, 2 GB of memory, and a 10 GB virtual disk. Nothing elaborate. I needed a target I could inspect, modify, stop, and restart without disturbing my workstation.

After provisioning the VM, I installed the build dependencies, cloned the OpenPLC v3 repository, installed the Linux runtime, and started the application.

The management dashboard was then accessible from my host workstation over HTTP.

With the target operational, I could begin mapping its exposed services and deciding where to start.

I started from the host workstation with network reconnaissance. The immediate objective was to identify the services listening on the target and determine which ones might provide a route into the OpenPLC deployment.

The HTTP application was served by Werkzeug on port 8080. Modbus TCP was reachable on port 502, and SSH was available on port 22.

That last service would become particularly important later. At this point, however, I was more interested in the management application. It was the obvious place to begin examining how programs were uploaded, compiled, and started.

I began inspecting the HTTP application and its routes.

Several endpoints redirected unauthenticated requests to the login page. These included routes associated with program management, hardware configuration, compilation logs, and application settings.

My next objective was to reproduce the relevant dashboard operations through HTTP requests. If I could automate the deployment workflow, I could use it to deliver and execute a modified control program. That was the plan, anyway.

I started interacting with the management interface programmatically.

Authentication worked. I obtained a session and explored the endpoints involved in program management and compilation. The intention was to reproduce the sequence that would normally happen through the browser, including triggering compilation.

Then the session behavior began getting in the way.

During my attempts to trigger compilation, the session kept getting refreshed or invalidated. Subsequent requests were redirected to the login page, interrupting the sequence. I could authenticate and reach the management interface, but I couldn't get the automated workflow to proceed consistently.

It was an irritating obstacle. I spent time trying to work around it, but I wasn't getting a reliable result.

There is something worth preserving here, though. I observed session-related interruptions while automating the management workflow. I did not establish the underlying cause, nor did I demonstrate a vulnerability in OpenPLC's session-management implementation.

I had another option sitting right in front of me.

The HTTP dashboard was exposed. I had authenticated successfully. The normal program-management workflow was available through the browser. I could upload a replacement program, compile it, and start the runtime.

I mean, it was straightforward, but then I hesitated.

The dashboard route felt almost too obvious. I wanted to know whether the same result could be achieved through another access path, particularly one that interacted with the host rather than relying on the management application.

During reconnaissance, I had also identified SSH on the target. I started wondering whether I could use it to perform the same operations directly. I didn't have a complete attack plan. I wasn't sitting there with a finished sequence of commands. It was just a question: Could I do this through SSH instead?

That question sent the investigation in a different direction.

SSH provided a way to interact with the Ubuntu host independently of the Flask dashboard.

For this experiment, I adopted a specific threat scenario: an attacker had already obtained valid SSH credentials for an account with sufficient privileges to modify the OpenPLC project and manage the runtime process. I was not attempting to steal credentials, bypass SSH authentication, or demonstrate an unauthenticated compromise. Those were outside the scope of this experiment.

What I wanted to establish was whether that level of host access could be used to substitute the active control logic and execute it.

The practical requirements began to take shape:

✔ Transfer a replacement Structured Text program to the target.✔ Replace the active project file in OpenPLC's storage directory.✔ Invoke the compilation pipeline.✔ Stop the existing runtime process.✔ Launch the newly compiled runtime.✔ Verify the modified program through Modbus TCP.

On paper, the sequence was fairly compact. Getting it to work was another matter.

One of the first obstacles appeared in the Structured Text program itself.

My replacement program kept failing during compilation. The error was particularly frustrating because the problem was a small syntactical difference at the end of the configuration block.

I had written: END CONFIGURATION but OpenPLC expected: END_CONFIGURATION. That underscore made all the difference.

What made this confusing was that my original baseline program also used END CONFIGURATION. It was already running in the lab, so I initially assumed the same structure would be accepted by the compiler. The existing runtime continued executing its previously compiled program, even though subsequent compilation attempts were reporting errors. That distinction wasn't immediately obvious to me.

I spent nearly an hour trying to understand what was wrong. I went through the source code, looking for an explanation, but the issue wasn't immediately apparent. Eventually, I examined the compiler's source more closely and traced the problem back to the expected syntax. It was a small detail, but it held up the entire experiment.

Once I corrected the terminator to END_CONFIGURATION, I could move forward with the deployment work.

There was no elegant shortcut. I kept investigating, adjusting the approach, and trying to make the individual operations work together. Eventually, I had enough of the deployment process understood to automate it.

I created a Structured Text payload named malicious_blink.st.

The program needed to produce an observable change. I didn't need an elaborate control routine; I needed a small piece of logic that would make it possible to distinguish the modified program from the baseline.

This maps the variable to memory word zero in the OpenPLC process image.

The payload uses a counter-based mechanism to toggle the value of ExploitTrigger between zero and one after every five execution cycles. This gave me a predictable state change that I could inspect externally through Modbus TCP.

The payload was ready. The remaining task was to get it into the active project, compile it, and bring the runtime back up.

I built a Python script called deploy_and_verify.py to automate the SSH-based workflow.

It used SCP to transfer the payload and SSH to perform the privileged operations on the target. The script handled the replacement of the active project file, compilation, and runtime restart.

The script first staged malicious_blink.st on the target VM.

This left the local research payload separate from the active OpenPLC project until the replacement step.

The staged file was copied into OpenPLC's Structured Text storage directory:

The script then replaced the active Structured Text file.

With the replacement file in place, the script invoked OpenPLC's compilation pipeline.

The compiler generated the C source files and supporting artifacts required to build the runtime:

One line in the output was particularly relevant:

The compiler had recognized the located memory variable and its integer type. The compilation then completed successfully.

This was an important checkpoint. The replacement logic had made it through the compilation process.

After compilation, the script terminated the existing core/openplc process and launched the newly compiled runtime binary.

The difference here matters. This was a process restart, not a live update of an executing control program. The old runtime was stopped, and the newly compiled binary was started.

The terminal output showed that the payload had been staged, the compilation had completed, and the runtime had been reloaded successfully. Now I needed to verify what was actually executing.

A successful compiler run did not, by itself, prove that the modified logic was executing. I needed an independent observation from the runtime.

Before deploying the replacement program, I had queried two holding registers through Modbus TCP. Both returned zero. I retained a screenshot of that baseline observation.

After the deployment, I ran the same query:

This queried two 16-bit holding registers, beginning at reference 1024.

Register 1024 alternated between zero and one. Register 1025 remained at zero. All six Modbus requests received valid responses, with no frame loss.

The compiler output and the Modbus observations support the result together.

The compiler identified the located variable as __MW0 with type INT. After the replacement program was compiled and the runtime restarted, the holding register associated with that variable began changing as expected.

In this lab configuration, %MW0 was observable through Modbus TCP at holding register 1024.

The baseline observation showed both queried registers at zero. Following deployment, register 1024 began alternating between zero and one. That behavior matched the payload's intended operation.

This is evidence that the replacement logic was compiled, loaded by the restarted runtime, and executing in a way that changed the exposed process image.

I did not connect physical PLC hardware or an actuator to the experiment. The demonstrated result was a modification of the software PLC's process image, observed through its Modbus interface. I am not claiming a physical process response.

The experiment established a working host-level path for unauthorized control-logic modification in my OpenPLC v3 lab.

With valid SSH credentials and sufficient privileges, the deployment could be modified remotely. The proof of concept performed the following operations:

The important finding concerns the trust placed in the host environment surrounding the SoftPLC.

The management dashboard is one way to deploy control logic. It is not the only component capable of affecting what ultimately executes. Project files reside on the host. Compilation happens there. The runtime is a host process. Anyone who obtains sufficient control over those components may be able to change the program that the SoftPLC executes.

SSH being reachable does not automatically make a SoftPLC vulnerable to control-logic substitution.

The attack path I demonstrated required valid credentials and enough privileges to modify the project, invoke compilation, and manage the runtime. Without those conditions, the specific workflow would not have been possible as implemented.

There are several ways an attacker might obtain credentials in a real environment: a compromised administrator workstation, credential reuse, credentials exposed in automation scripts, accidental disclosure, or misuse of an account that already has administrative privileges. Those are plausible acquisition scenarios, not findings from this experiment. I did not test them.

The demonstrated weakness lies in what an attacker can do after obtaining the required host access. If SSH access is insufficiently restricted and a privileged account is compromised, the attacker may gain the ability to replace the control logic itself.

The initial investigation focused on the HTTP management application. The final proof of concept took another route.

I did not exploit the dashboard's upload endpoint, bypass its authentication, or rely on its manual deployment workflow. I used SSH to interact with the underlying operating system and modify the active OpenPLC project directly. These are distinct access paths with different security boundaries.

A dashboard-based attack would depend on access to the management application and its deployment functions. The SSH-based route depends on host authentication and operating-system privileges. The latter was the path I successfully demonstrated.

The results need to be understood within the boundaries of the experiment.

These boundaries describe what was and was not established. The host-level control-logic substitution itself was demonstrated.

I started with Beremiz, spent nearly nine hours trying to understand its internals, and eventually changed targets. OpenPLC v3 gave me a more accessible environment, although the first approach I tried there didn't work as smoothly as I had hoped.

I initially attempted to automate the management interface. The session interruptions and repeated redirects made that workflow unreliable. The dashboard itself was available, and I could have used it directly. Instead, I wondered whether SSH could provide another route.

That question cost me another seven hours.

I had to work out how to stage the replacement program, identify the active project file, invoke the compiler, and restart the runtime remotely. Once those pieces came together, I automated the process and ran it against the target.

The compiler completed successfully. The runtime restarted. Modbus polling showed the expected changes in the process image.

The experiment demonstrated that an attacker with valid SSH credentials and sufficient host privileges could substitute the active control logic in this OpenPLC v3 deployment, compile it, and execute it without using the dashboard's manual upload workflow.

There is a broader lesson here for SoftPLC deployments. The security of the control runtime cannot be considered separately from the machine hosting it. Administrative access, project-file integrity, compiler execution, and runtime management all influence what logic eventually runs.

Understanding Software PLCs: Architecture, Execution, and Security Boundaries

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

#9671. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. #9667. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

150Sec focuses on thought-provoking stories around Europe’s emerging startup scenes.

150Sec focuses on thought-provoking stories around Europe’s emerging startup scenes.

150Sec focuses on thought-provoking stories around Europe’s emerging startup scenes.

The Alphabet-owned company made the request to the General Court in Luxembourg on Tuesday, September 29, Reuters reported. On the same day, it also sued the European Commission over the July decision behind the order, which was issued under the Digital Markers Act (DMA).

The request raises the stakes, as filing an appeal does not pause the order. So, unless judges grant temporary relief, Google must start sharing data in January 2027, likely long before the court rules on the substances of the case.

Under the Commission’s decision, Google must give eligible rivals anonymized ranking, query, click and view data on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. AI chatbots that offer search functions qualify, and Google must share the same data it uses to improve its own search engine.

The tech giant must furthermore complete key technical preparations this year before data sharing begins.

Google can also refuse to share with any recipient it judges to pose a serious cybersecurity or data-protection risk.

Google is also contesting a second July decision that requires it to give rival AI assistants the same access as Gemini to 11 Android features, including voice activation, by August 2027.

Bethel stressed that the order would “weaken vital security protections on Android”.

How the court handles the suspension request will be an early signal of how far the DMA can reach into the core of Big Tech platforms. Until then, the Commission’s clock keeps running.

#9659. Code From Your Phone with Codex: Complete Beginner Walkthrough

Developer & PhD Researcher in AI · 20+ Years in Web, Data & Growth · Helping Developers Work Smarter with AI

Developer & PhD Researcher in AI · 20+ Years in Web, Data & Growth · Helping Developers Work Smarter with AI

Developer & PhD Researcher in AI · 20+ Years in Web, Data & Growth · Helping Developers Work Smarter with AI

A coding task can need your attention while you are away from your computer. The agent may be waiting for a command approval, a decision about scope, or a review of the changes it made.

Codex in the ChatGPT mobile app lets you handle those parts from your phone. You choose a connected computer and project, send the task, follow its progress, and inspect the result. The code still runs on the selected computer.

In my demo, I use this setup with an image-generator project. I ask Codex to explain the code, suggest an improvement, write a plan, and implement it. Codex reports eleven passing offline tests, then I ask for a browser preview so I can check the interface too.

Below is the complete setup and review workflow, including the screenshot workaround for an app running at localhost. Start with a small change and a project you can verify.

Get the apps from the official ChatGPT download page. Open Codex on your computer and make sure your project is available there before pairing.

OpenAI's current remote setup guide lists Mac and Windows hosts, with iOS and Android clients depending on rollout. The phone steps here show my iPhone. Some app versions still call the feature Remote instead of Codex. A workspace admin may also need to enable Remote Control. Check the supported setup and requirements if your menus differ.

You start this setup in the desktop app. Installing only the Codex CLI or IDE extension won't give you the pairing screen.

Scan your own code. The code in my recording is hidden.

On your phone, scan the code with the camera. Open the ChatGPT link, check the account and workspace, and approve the connection. Complete any passkey, SSO, or multi-factor authentication prompt it shows.

Each pairing connects a particular device to a particular computer. Repeat setup if you want another phone to control another host. You can manage paired devices in the computer's Connections settings. Official pairing instructions

Enable Keep this PC awake, or the equivalent option, if available. Leave the desktop app open and your computer connected to power. A sleeping or offline computer can't do the work you send it.

Now open Codex in the ChatGPT mobile sidebar. Your connected computer should appear. In the video, I also use Face ID or the device passcode to protect access on my phone.

My mobile home screen has All, Cloud, and a filter for my computer, followed by saved chats.

Choose your connected computer for this walkthrough.

Select your computer to use its project files and installed tools. Cloud runs work in a separate cloud environment; it doesn't automatically have the files sitting on your laptop. For that setup, see my Codex Cloud tutorial. Both options are available through the Codex mobile workflow, subject to account and workspace availability.

Start a new chat and select a project. You may also see Don't work in a project, but selecting the folder you want to change makes this tutorial easier to follow.

Before sending anything, check the computer and project names. It's easy to open a familiar chat and forget which machine it belongs to.

Open the model controls to choose a model and reasoning effort. In my recording, I use High. You can begin with the available default; matching my exact model isn't necessary.

Next, open the approval settings. My version shows:

The approval options shown in my demo. Host and workspace policies still apply.

I use Approve for me in the video. Choose the narrowest access that works for your task, and read a requested command before approving it. Automatic review doesn't make every action harmless.

For your first attempt, you can make the request more specific:

Start by understanding the project before asking for changes.

You can follow progress and expand activity entries to inspect commands. In my recording, Codex looks for AGENTS.md, the file where a project can keep instructions for coding agents. It then summarizes the code and how to run it.

Read the suggestions and choose one manageable change. Asking for every improvement at once makes the result much harder to review on a phone.

In the demo, I ask for a plan with an achievable goal. Codex proposes shared input checks and faster loading of saved image-generation history. The plan includes a goal, scope, checklist, and Done when conditions.

A small scope gives you something concrete to check afterward.

Here's a reusable version of that request:

You can also enable Plan mode from the plus menu. Pursue goal is useful for an outcome that needs several rounds of work. A written checklist alone doesn't mean you've started a persistent goal. My Codex goal guide explains that workflow.

While Codex works, use Queue for a follow-up that can wait. Use Steer when you need to correct the current direction. For example, “Keep this change inside the settings page” belongs in the current work, not after a large rewrite. OpenAI explains these controls in its remote engineering guide.

The result in my recording has two parts: Codex reports that all 11 offline tests pass, and it says browser UI verification is still outstanding. Read both. A passing test report gives you evidence about the checks that ran; the unfinished browser review tells you what to do next.

Passing tests and checking the interface are separate parts of the review.

I ask Codex to start the project. It runs on the computer at localhost, using port 8765 in this example.

Opening that address on the phone doesn't open the computer's app. Localhost means the device opening the address. On your phone, it points back to your phone.

My workaround is to ask Codex for screenshots. Try:

In the recording, Codex uses a headless browser, a browser running without a visible window, to capture the app. The images appear in the chat, where I can open and zoom into them.

Check whether buttons fit, text is readable, and the layout works on a narrow screen. Screenshots show appearance; ask for interaction checks too. If Codex lacks browser tools on your host, it needs that setup before it can capture the app.

Open Changes to inspect the diff: the lines added, removed, or edited. Use Files when you need more context. Ask Codex to explain anything you don't understand before committing.

If you expected an existing repository, first check that you selected the correct folder. For a new project, open a terminal in that project's root and run:

Before the first commit, check .gitignore so secrets such as .env files, dependencies, and generated output stay out of Git. Then ask Codex:

A commit saves a checkpoint in your local Git history. Pushing sends commits to a remote repository such as GitHub. Deploying publishes the application. Treat them as separate steps, so you know exactly what you've approved.

Type / in the composer to see the commands your version supports. The most useful starting points are /plan for planning, /review for checking changes, /side for a side question, and /status for session details. Availability depends on your app, account, and host. Mobile command reference

Attach a screenshot when describing a visual problem. “This button overlaps the title” is much easier to act on when Codex can see it.

Rename chats around the task, pin active work, and archive finished chats from the three-dot menu. A name like “Fix mobile menu” is easier to find later than “New chat.”

If your computer is missing, check that the desktop app is running, connections are enabled, and both devices use the same account and workspace. Update both apps and pair again if needed.

If a session disconnects, check the computer's power and network first. Keeping the phone awake won't help if the host has gone to sleep.

If you can't find Codex or Remote, check feature availability and your workspace's Remote Control settings. Signing out can also turn Remote Control off; enable it again after signing in. OpenAI keeps the connection troubleshooting steps in its setup guide.

The part I would repeat is the review sequence: give Codex a specific task, check its plan, read what it tested, and inspect the result before committing. On a phone, keep the change small enough that you can make those decisions carefully. If a diff needs a larger screen, leave that review for your computer.

How to Use Codex Cloud: From GitHub Setup to Your First Pull Request

Whether you're a social media influencer, marketer, or business owner, keeping up with the constant need for fresh, engaging content can be overwhelming. That's where AI tools come in – they're not just fancy tech, they're your secret weapon for creating better content faster.

Let's Dive Into the Top 10 AI Tools for 2025

What Makes It Special: ChatGPT has evolved into a comprehensive content creation assistant by combining advanced language understanding with specialized content optimization features. Its ability to generate, edit, and optimize content while maintaining brand voice and industry expertise makes it an essential tool for creators who need to produce high-quality written content at scale.

What Makes It Special: Canva Magic Studio has transformed the graphic design landscape by combining its user-friendly interface with powerful AI capabilities. Perfect For: Small businesses, social media managers, and anyone needing quick, professional-looking designs.

What Makes It Special: RunwayML stands out as the ultimate video creation powerhouse by combining professional-grade effects with user-friendly AI technology. Its game-changing ability to manipulate video content – from changing weather effects with a text prompt to removing objects seamlessly in real-time – makes it indispensable for creators who want to produce high-quality video content without getting bogged down by technical complexities.

Perfect For: Video creators, YouTubers, and social media managers who want to create professional-quality videos quickly.

What Makes It Special: Midjourney V6 has redefined AI image generation by mastering the nuances of professional photography and artistic style. Perfect For: Social media managers, digital marketers, and anyone needing professional-quality visuals consistently.

What Makes It Special: Synthesia has transformed video creation by making it possible to create professional-looking AI avatar videos in minutes. Its ability to clone voices accurately and generate multiple languages with proper accents and inflections makes it the ultimate tool for creators who need professional-quality voiceovers without the traditional recording process or voice actor limitations.

Perfect For: Podcasters, video creators, and content creators needing professional voiceovers in multiple languages.

What Makes It Special: Tribescaler brings a scientific approach to viral content creation by combining trend analysis with content optimization. Its powerful AI engine analyzes successful content patterns across platforms and provides actionable insights to help creators craft content that's more likely to go viral, while maintaining authenticity and audience engagement.

Perfect For: Content creators and social media managers focused on maximizing reach and engagement.

What Makes It Special: CopyAI has established itself as a powerhouse in AI-powered copywriting by offering specialized content generation for various marketing formats. Its sophisticated understanding of marketing psychology and brand voice, combined with its ability to generate compelling copy across multiple formats and industries, makes it invaluable for marketers and content creators who need to produce engaging, conversion-focused content at scale.

Perfect For: Marketing teams, copywriters, and businesses needing high-converting marketing copy across multiple channels.

The AI tools listed here are revolutionizing the content creation landscape in 2025, making it easier than ever to produce high-quality, engaging, and impactful content. By integrating these tools into your workflow, you can save time, unleash your creativity, and achieve better results.

AI doesn't replace creativity; it amplifies it. As a content creator, your unique voice and vision are irreplaceable. These tools serve as enablers, helping you focus on what you do best—creating. #9649. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.
